Scope it all out below. Amazon is delivering the first pre-order discounts on Apple’s new HomeView , as we detailed already, but it has also now undercut everyone on the next-generation Apple TV 4K . Amazon is now offering the first discount on Apple TV 4K pre-orders at $289.99 shipped . All of that, combined with the fact that shipping times have slipped significantly at Apple for the new Apple TV 4K – some locations can’t get a pre-order delivered until late November at this point – make this Amazon offer all the more sweeter; Amazon is delivering Apple TV 4K pre-orders faster than Apple and for less now. As of the time of writing, Amazon can still land the new Apple TV on your doorstep on launch day – November 13. This is also true for the new Apple TV Siri Remote (for folks not updating their existing Apple TV unit) and the new HomeView. Delivery times for the new HomeView at Apple are starting to slip into December at this point – Amazon is selling them for less and shipping it on day one still if you’re quick. At some point soon, you’ll be lucky to get a HomeView shipped straight from Apple before December, and the silver model has already sold out at Amazon – you’ll want to get in there quick if you want one: Amazon is still offering a couple colors with an early pre-order discount and shipping them on launch day in mid November, but it’s only a matter of time before they are either completely sold out or tough to get for launch day. As of right now only the Starlight, Space Gray, and Rose Pink are available with launch day delivery on Amazon, and only the latter two are carrying the pre-order discount. Consider this a bit of PSA and get in there now if you plan on getting one at a deal or before December. Just after pre-order discounts went live on the new HomeView , alongside the next-gen Apple TV 4K , Apple’s all-new iPhone Duo is set to go up for pre-order this morning at 8 a.m. ET. You can, of course, get one straight from Apple if you get in there quick, but you might want to explore your options at Best Buy as well – it is offering packages starting at just $55 per month and as much as $1,200 off with trade-ins . As per usual, if you’re looking for a complete unlocked iPhone Duo, you’re going to need to go straight to Apple . However, Best Buy does get competitive with monthly plan options and rates when it comes to brand new iPhone releases and it appears to be doing so for Duo this morning. Best Buy is also offering some trade-in action on the new Duo as well – you can score $1,200 off the total cost of the phone with an iPhone 17 Pro or Pro Max trade, for example. You’ll, of course, want to double check the trade-in value Apple will offer you, but Best Buy can get aggressive with trade-in values as well. These Best Buy iPhone Duo pre-order deals are, admittedly, going to be limited time to some degree, simply because of the carrier options, but they can actually net you the impressive new Apple foldable for much less out of pocket now than paying $2,000+ straight to Apple this morning. We are still tracking a giant $600 price drop on this more pricey 2TB M5 Pro model, but Amazon is now offering Apple’s most affordable 24GB M5 Pro MacBook Pro at the lowest prices in months as well – it is now sitting at $430 off the list. Amazon is now offering the 14-inch M5 Pro MacBook Pro with 24GB of RAM and the 1TB SSD down at $2,069.10 shipped with the Space Black livery. This machine carries a $2,499 list price and is now $430 off . We seen this same deal pop up a couple times in the last couple weeks before quickly jumping back up in price, so there’s no telling how long this deal might stick around for. The price we are seeing here today is on par with the lowest we have tracked on Amazon in months. It now joins a pair of particularly notable discounts live on higher-end Pros as well: Apple has officially unleashed the new HomeView smart display and HomePod mini 2 for pre-order, as well as the new, and particularly expensive Apple TV 4K . If you are not ready to drop $299 for the upgraded Apple TV experience, you can at least upgrade your existing setup with the all-new Apple TV Siri Remote (4th generation) for just $59 . No, this is not technically a deal by any means – $59 is the list price on the new Siri Remote. But if history is any indication deals on this thing are going to be incredibly rare and it’s a whole lot less pricey than buying a whole new Apple TV 4K that includes this same remote. The new Apple TV Siri Remote (4th generation) is not only compatible with new Apple TV 4th Gen, but also the Apple TV HD and the previous-generation Apple TV 4K. Alongside pre-orders for the new HomeView smart display , HomePod mini 2 , and Apple TV 4K , this month ushered in all-time low pricing on the 2026 Magic Keyboard you might need for your new M6 Mac mini. And it is still down at the Prime Day all-time low . Considering how rare deals can be at times on Apple’s official Magic accessories, we wanted to highlight this deal on the new all-glyph model once again while it is still live. Regularly $99, you can pick one up over at Amazon down at $79.99 shipped right now. That might not seem like a notable discount, but when it comes to Magic Apple accessories, especially this soon after release, it is. The new HomeView smart display , next-generation Apple TV 4K , and HomePod mini 2 are now available for pre-order, but we are also tracking all-time low pricing across the latest Apple iPhone 18 Pro case lineup . Select models, like the new Olive 18 Pro Silicone case have now dropped again to a new Amazon all-time low at 25% off, and you’ll find loads more with deals below. While most colors and models are still at the Prime Day lows we featured last week, the Apple iPhone 18 Pro Silicone Case with MagSafe in the new Olive colorway has now dropped even lower to $36.75 shipped . That’s 25% off the regular $49 list price and the lowest price we have tracked to date. extraction.body: Earlier this week, Apple announced its new Apple TV 4K, which costs nearly twice as much as the 2022 model did at launch. Amazon is now offering the first discount on the forthcoming streaming box (coming out on November 13th), just days after discounting Apple’s new smart display for the first time. Right now, you can preorder the latest Apple TV 4K ahead of its November 13th release date for $289.99 ($9 off) at Amazon. Unlike its predecessors, though, the new model features far-field microphones so you can quickly make hands-free requests. You can, for example, ask for recommendations, like nature documentaries available on Apple TV, or ask questions about what you’re watching. Siri AI can also understand personal context, too, so long as you have an iPhone or iPad connected to your account that supports Apple Intelligence. Apple has made a few other welcome upgrades, though — as my colleague John Higgins points out — not as many as some may have expected. While Apple skipped features we’d hope to see on a $300 streamer, like audio passthrough and support for 120fps output, it’s nice that the Siri Remote now supports Find My precision tracking, so you can make it ring when it goes missing or use the Find My app on your iPhone to pinpoint its location. The new Apple TV 4K also supports a more expansive surround-sound setup, allowing you to pair up to four compatible HomePod speakers instead of just two. Read our hands-on impressions of the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K. Three more Verge-approved deals: * If you’ve been meaning to pick up Pikmin 4, Walmart is selling a digital copy for $39.88 ($20 off), which is a great price considering most other retailers are still charging the full $59.99. It’s the original Switch version, but you can upgrade to the forthcoming Nintendo Switch 2 Edition when it arrives on November 12th by purchasing a separate $9.99 upgrade pack, which adds improved graphics and a new Dandori Academy mode. That brings your total to just $49.87, saving you about $20 compared to buying the $69.99 Switch 2 Edition outright. I currently use the OtterBox Symmetry Series Clear Case for my iPhone 16, which normally costs $49.99 but is now available in various colors for just $5.99 with a 90-day warranty. The sale also includes cases for other iPhones, as well as some Samsung and Google phones, so it’s worth browsing even if you’re not planning to upgrade your phone anytime soon. * Fanttik’s S1 Pro electric screwdriver is on sale for $45.99 ($44 off) at Amazon, which is $5 shy of its best price to date. It’s a handy cordless option for small tasks ranging from tightening screws to assembling desks, with 16 S2 hardened steel bits for tackling a variety of jobs. The USB-C rechargeable screwdriver also comes with a 220RPM motor and three torque settings, along with a LED light to help illuminate your workspace.

extraction.body: Earlier this week, Apple announced its new Apple TV 4K, which costs nearly twice as much as the 2022 model did at launch. Amazon is now offering the first discount on the forthcoming streaming box (coming out on November 13th), just days after discounting Apple’s new smart display for the first time. Right now, you can preorder the latest Apple TV 4K ahead of its November 13th release date for $289.99 ($9 off) at Amazon. Unlike its predecessors, though, the new model features far-field microphones so you can quickly make hands-free requests. You can, for example, ask for recommendations, like nature documentaries available on Apple TV, or ask questions about what you’re watching. Siri AI can also understand personal context, too, so long as you have an iPhone or iPad connected to your account that supports Apple Intelligence. Apple has made a few other welcome upgrades, though — as my colleague John Higgins points out — not as many as some may have expected. While Apple skipped features we’d hope to see on a $300 streamer, like audio passthrough and support for 120fps output, it’s nice that the Siri Remote now supports Find My precision tracking, so you can make it ring when it goes missing or use the Find My app on your iPhone to pinpoint its location. The new Apple TV 4K also supports a more expansive surround-sound setup, allowing you to pair up to four compatible HomePod speakers instead of just two. Read our hands-on impressions of the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K. Three more Verge-approved deals: * If you’ve been meaning to pick up Pikmin 4, Walmart is selling a digital copy for $39.88 ($20 off), which is a great price considering most other retailers are still charging the full $59.99. It’s the original Switch version, but you can upgrade to the forthcoming Nintendo Switch 2 Edition when it arrives on November 12th by purchasing a separate $9.99 upgrade pack, which adds improved graphics and a new Dandori Academy mode. That brings your total to just $49.87, saving you about $20 compared to buying the $69.99 Switch 2 Edition outright. I currently use the OtterBox Symmetry Series Clear Case for my iPhone 16, which normally costs $49.99 but is now available in various colors for just $5.99 with a 90-day warranty. The sale also includes cases for other iPhones, as well as some Samsung and Google phones, so it’s worth browsing even if you’re not planning to upgrade your phone anytime soon. * Fanttik’s S1 Pro electric screwdriver is on sale for $45.99 ($44 off) at Amazon, which is $5 shy of its best price to date. It’s a handy cordless option for small tasks ranging from tightening screws to assembling desks, with 16 S2 hardened steel bits for tackling a variety of jobs. The USB-C rechargeable screwdriver also comes with a 220RPM motor and three torque settings, along with a LED light to help illuminate your workspace.

sources.title: OpenAI models hacked a crypto wallet and breached more websites
passages: OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts.
In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly.

In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site’s file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said .
“It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint’s authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied.
In one evaluation, the changes let the model make an internal search tool relay queries to the public dashboard.
OpenAI researchers had prompted the agents to retrieve only five dashboard figures.
Even after resetting the setting, the model continued using the token to retrieve non-public data.
“All five answers in this evaluation were marked incorrect.”
It has become common for researchers and journalists to describe incidents like these as AI “going rogue.” That’s not necessarily true.

While prompts fed to the models didn’t instruct them to use the alternate methods for completing their objectives, models are trained to be efficient, steadfastly persistent, and, when possible, to find shortcuts that lessen workloads.
During reinforcement-learning training, the model had been prompted to seek public trade statistics.

sources.title: OpenAI says its AI models escaped control and hacked into AI company Hugging Face - Fortune
passages: Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a statement provided to OpenAI for its Tuesday blog post about the incident that his company is “grateful for the collaboration with OpenAI on this and other topics.
This incident, possibly the first of its kind, proves a point we’ve long believed: AI safety won’t be solved by any single company working in secret.
But in those incidents, while the model hacked its way out of its controlled environment, it did not hack its way into any other company’s systems.
OpenAI did not say when these other incidents occurred, but we know now that this same model was one of the Hugging Face attackers.

OpenAI rival Anthropic has also reported that its Mythos model escaped a sandbox and gained internet access it was not supposed to have during safety testing in order to email a researcher about a task.

It said the models were being used in an internal test designed to evaluate their cyber security capabilities and that they were being tested without guardrails in place that might normally limit the models’ ability to conduct cyber attacks.
OpenAI is still working on implementing better controls in its research environment, even if it means slowing down its research, until it can patch the vulnerabilities.
The company said it is also continuing to work with Hugging Face to help it bolster its defenses.
Hugging Face has not said which American AI model it tried to use to defend its networks initially.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic have released versions of their most capable AI models with guardrails that limit access to cyber capabilities while also announcing programs for select, vetted partners who can use more capable versions of those models for cyber defense.
So far, what they know is the models began the attack by gaining internet access.
This required spending a “substantial amount of inference compute,” as well as exploiting a zero-day vulnerability in internally hosted third-party software.
OpenAI has now disclosed this zero-day to the vendor.
By that time, Hugging Face had already identified and contained the attack, and had begun piecing together what happened.

It is thought to be one of just a handful of incidents recorded so far involving AI agents acting autonomously to carry out an attack, a risk cyber security experts have been warning about for the past year as AI models have become increasingly adept at both coding and carrying out long-running tasks.
In one example, the model executed a complex, multi-part attack to get into Hugging Face servers, using exposed credentials and zero-day vulnerabilities.
OpenAI said that it considered this to be “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities, and are responding accordingly.”
Jeremy Kahn is the AI editor at Fortune , spearheading the publication's coverage of artificial intelligence.
He also co-authors Eye on AI , Fortune ’s flagship AI newsletter.

extraction.body: OpenAI said Tuesday that two of its AI models autonomously hacked their way out of a controlled environment where they were supposed to be walled off from internet access and then hacked their way into the systems of Hugging Face, a company that hosts open source AI models and testing resources, in order to cheat on an internal evaluation test. OpenAI disclosed the incident in a blog post on Tuesday, a stunning announcement that is certain to set off alarm bells across the industry about the increasing power of AI models and the risk of them going rogue. According to OpenAI, the incident involved “a combination” of both its latest and most powerful publicly-available model, GPT-5.6 Sol, as well as an even more powerful unreleased model. It said the models were being used in an internal test designed to evaluate their cyber security capabilities and that they were being tested without guardrails in place that might normally limit the models’ ability to conduct cyber attacks. The models were being tested against a freely-available cybersecurity benchmark evaluation called ExploitGym. The models, accordingly to OpenAI, correctly surmised that the solutions to that test were maintained by Hugging Face. “The models identified and chained vulnerabilities across OpenAI’s research environment and Hugging Face’s production infrastructure to obtain test solutions directly from Hugging Face’s production database,” OpenAI said in its blog post. “All evidence suggests that the models were hyperfocused on finding a solution for ExploitGym, going to extreme lengths to achieve a rather narrow testing goal.” OpenAI said that it considered this to be “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities, and are responding accordingly.” Cybersecurity researchers have long been warning that advanced AI systems are capable of such attacks. Roman Yampolskiy, an AI safety researcher and computer science professor at the University of Louisville, says this example highlights how powerful models “can discover and exploit vulnerabilities in ways that were not explicitly anticipated by their developers.” He expects to see more incidents of this type because AI models “are fundamentally unpredictable and ultimately uncontrollable.” Hugging Face disclosed in a blog post on Thursday that it had been the victim of a cyber attack earlier in the week that it believed was conducted by an autonomous AI agent. It is thought to be one of just a handful of incidents recorded so far involving AI agents acting autonomously to carry out an attack, a risk cyber security experts have been warning about for the past year as AI models have become increasingly adept at both coding and carrying out long-running tasks. At the time, Hugging Face said it was continuing to investigate the attack and did not know who had carried it out. It said that it had first attempted to use an undisclosed AI model for a leading U.S. lab to defend against the attacking AI agent but that the guardrails around that model’s cyber capabilities stymied its response team’s work. The company said it instead wound up using an open source AI model from Chinese company Z.ai to carry out its defense. Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a statement provided to OpenAI for its Tuesday blog post about the incident that his company is “grateful for the collaboration with OpenAI on this and other topics. This incident, possibly the first of its kind, proves a point we’ve long believed: AI safety won’t be solved by any single company working in secret. It will be solved in the open, collaboratively, with broad access to AI for every defender, everywhere.” Earlier this week, OpenAI published a different blog post about the same unreleased, powerful model, saying it had also escaped its internal sandboxes—environments where AI models have no internet access and often have limited software tools that they can call—during other testing. But in those incidents, while the model hacked its way out of its controlled environment, it did not hack its way into any other company’s systems. OpenAI did not say when these other incidents occurred, but we know now that this same model was one of the Hugging Face attackers. OpenAI rival Anthropic has also reported that its Mythos model escaped a sandbox and gained internet access it was not supposed to have during safety testing in order to email a researcher about a task. OpenAI and Hugging Face are continuing to investigate the issue, and will share more when that process is complete. So far, what they know is the models began the attack by gaining internet access. This required spending a “substantial amount of inference compute,” as well as exploiting a zero-day vulnerability in internally hosted third-party software. OpenAI has now disclosed this zero-day to the vendor. After the models got web access, they went to Hugging Face to find answers to ExploitGym, assuming the platform would have models, datasets, and solutions that they could use to cheat its way to high performance on the benchmark. In one example, the model executed a complex, multi-part attack to get into Hugging Face servers, using exposed credentials and zero-day vulnerabilities. OpenAI detected the Hugging Face attack and reached out to Hugging Face to disclose it. By that time, Hugging Face had already identified and contained the attack, and had begun piecing together what happened. The incident is not over. OpenAI is still working on implementing better controls in its research environment, even if it means slowing down its research, until it can patch the vulnerabilities. The company said it is also continuing to work with Hugging Face to help it bolster its defenses. As part of that effort, OpenAI said it has now added Hugging Face to its “trusted access” cybersecurity program. That means that Hugging Face will be able to use a version of OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model that has fewer guardrails around cyber capabilities and which is designed to help cyber defenders. Hugging Face has not said which American AI model it tried to use to defend its networks initially. Both OpenAI and Anthropic have released versions of their most capable AI models with guardrails that limit access to cyber capabilities while also announcing programs for select, vetted partners who can use more capable versions of those models for cyber defense. Jeremy Kahn is the AI editor at Fortune , spearheading the publication's coverage of artificial intelligence. He also co-authors Eye on AI , Fortune ’s flagship AI newsletter.

passages: California Subpoenas OpenAI Over AI Models That Hacked Their Way Out of a Test

California Attorney General Rob Bonta said Thursday that his office served OpenAI with an investigative subpoena on Wednesday, seeking answers about cybersecurity incidents involving its AI models, according to his office .

OpenAI is headquartered in California, and when Bonta declined to oppose its shift to a for-profit structure in October 2025, he said his office would keep "a close eye on OpenAI" to protect "the safety of all Californians."
Brenna Bird , Iowa's attorney general, led a 15-state coalition in August demanding that OpenAI preserve records and be transparent about the hack.
Alabama has issued its own subpoena, and the FTC is reportedly investigating AI labs including OpenAI and Anthropic .

extraction.body: California Subpoenas OpenAI Over AI Models That Hacked Their Way Out of a Test California Attorney General Rob Bonta said Thursday that his office served OpenAI with an investigative subpoena on Wednesday, seeking answers about cybersecurity incidents involving its AI models, according to his office . “My office is asking OpenAI additional questions regarding cybersecurity incidents and risks involving the company and its AI models,” said Attorney General Bonta. “Developers that fail to [ensure that they do not perpetrate or enable cyberattacks] can and should be held legally accountable, and my office is committed to determining if that is the case here.” A subpoena is a legal order to hand over documents or answers, and ignoring one gets you in front of a judge. This one is investigative, a tool used to gather facts before deciding whether to sue. Bonta's office hasn't said publicly what it wants OpenAI to produce. Frontier models—the most advanced AI systems on the market—can be "legitimate tools for cyber defense," Bonta said. But the companies that build them have "a moral and legal responsibility" to make sure they don't carry out or enable cyberattacks, whether during testing or after release, he said. The subpoena follows a July incident that reads like bad science fiction. coreStoryFacts.text: Left without funds for a coding task, an OpenAI model spent test crypto from a stranger’s wallet and left it out of its report.
Copyright © 2026 SecurityWeek ®, a Wired Business Media Publication.

OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts.
In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly.

In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site’s file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said .
“It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint’s authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied.
In one evaluation, the changes let the model make an internal search tool relay queries to the public dashboard.
OpenAI researchers had prompted the agents to retrieve only five dashboard figures.
Even after resetting the setting, the model continued using the token to retrieve non-public data.
“All five answers in this evaluation were marked incorrect.”
It has become common for researchers and journalists to describe incidents like these as AI “going rogue.” That’s not necessarily true.

While prompts fed to the models didn’t instruct them to use the alternate methods for completing their objectives, models are trained to be efficient, steadfastly persistent, and, when possible, to find shortcuts that lessen workloads.
During reinforcement-learning training, the model had been prompted to seek public trade statistics.

Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a statement provided to OpenAI for its Tuesday blog post about the incident that his company is “grateful for the collaboration with OpenAI on this and other topics.
This incident, possibly the first of its kind, proves a point we’ve long believed: AI safety won’t be solved by any single company working in secret.
But in those incidents, while the model hacked its way out of its controlled environment, it did not hack its way into any other company’s systems.
OpenAI did not say when these other incidents occurred, but we know now that this same model was one of the Hugging Face attackers.

OpenAI rival Anthropic has also reported that its Mythos model escaped a sandbox and gained internet access it was not supposed to have during safety testing in order to email a researcher about a task.

It said the models were being used in an internal test designed to evaluate their cyber security capabilities and that they were being tested without guardrails in place that might normally limit the models’ ability to conduct cyber attacks.
OpenAI is still working on implementing better controls in its research environment, even if it means slowing down its research, until it can patch the vulnerabilities.
The company said it is also continuing to work with Hugging Face to help it bolster its defenses.
Hugging Face has not said which American AI model it tried to use to defend its networks initially.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic have released versions of their most capable AI models with guardrails that limit access to cyber capabilities while also announcing programs for select, vetted partners who can use more capable versions of those models for cyber defense.
So far, what they know is the models began the attack by gaining internet access.

The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale. It then made configuration changes on the server. In one evaluation, the changes let the model make an internal search tool relay queries to the public dashboard. In a second evaluation, the model downloaded five non-public tables containing 147,451 rows. OpenAI researchers had prompted the agents to retrieve only five dashboard figures. Even after resetting the setting, the model continued using the token to retrieve non-public data. “The evaluation ended without the model disclosing that it had guessed answers, accessed the organization’s internal systems, downloaded non-public tables, or changed the authentication configuration,” OpenAI said. “All five answers in this evaluation were marked incorrect.” In a third report , the company said a model prompted to update a cryptocurrency trading application used funds from a locked wallet on a test network. The model “derived wallet keys from publicly known developer recovery phrases, found an account with test-network funds, and used that account to pay for the requested contract deployment.” The report continued: “The model questioned whether it had permission, then reasoned that a public recovery phrase and valueless test-network tokens made the funds acceptable to use. The deployment succeeded and charged transaction fees to the account. This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder’s permission, then act on that judgment without authorization.” In the last report , OpenAI said that a model bypassed restrictions researchers had placed on the types of web requests it could make. During reinforcement-learning training, the model had been prompted to seek public trade statistics. OpenAI went on: After finding a public yearbook and submitting an answer, it continued probing for another route to the statistics service. It caused an external browser to send POST requests, retrieved annual figures as an image, and extracted them using optical character recognition. It then developed a reusable helper that returned response text through a forwarding service and callback mailbox, repeatedly checked the retrieved figures, and used saved data in submitted responses. This case shows how a model can bypass restrictions on its own tools by getting external services to perform the blocked actions, even after finding another way to answer the question. The model first tried to use an external browser with permission to make GET requests on its behalf, then used JavaScript to obtain the information. The model then used an online mailbox to troubleshoot the technique. Eventually, the model settled on a different method: It asked the external browser to open a web form that sent the trade query to the statistics service by POST. While prompts fed to the models didn’t instruct them to use the alternate methods for completing their objectives, models are trained to be efficient, steadfastly persistent, and, when possible, to find shortcuts that lessen workloads. Further, most or all of the models had disabled certain guardrails that might have prevented the actions. In this sense, the models performed precisely as OpenAI had trained them to. sources.title: OpenAI says its AI models escaped control and hacked into AI company Hugging Face - Fortune
passages: Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a statement provided to OpenAI for its Tuesday blog post about the incident that his company is “grateful for the collaboration with OpenAI on this and other topics.
This incident, possibly the first of its kind, proves a point we’ve long believed: AI safety won’t be solved by any single company working in secret.
But in those incidents, while the model hacked its way out of its controlled environment, it did not hack its way into any other company’s systems.
OpenAI did not say when these other incidents occurred, but we know now that this same model was one of the Hugging Face attackers.

OpenAI rival Anthropic has also reported that its Mythos model escaped a sandbox and gained internet access it was not supposed to have during safety testing in order to email a researcher about a task.

It said the models were being used in an internal test designed to evaluate their cyber security capabilities and that they were being tested without guardrails in place that might normally limit the models’ ability to conduct cyber attacks.
OpenAI is still working on implementing better controls in its research environment, even if it means slowing down its research, until it can patch the vulnerabilities.
The company said it is also continuing to work with Hugging Face to help it bolster its defenses.
Hugging Face has not said which American AI model it tried to use to defend its networks initially.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic have released versions of their most capable AI models with guardrails that limit access to cyber capabilities while also announcing programs for select, vetted partners who can use more capable versions of those models for cyber defense.
So far, what they know is the models began the attack by gaining internet access.
This required spending a “substantial amount of inference compute,” as well as exploiting a zero-day vulnerability in internally hosted third-party software.
OpenAI has now disclosed this zero-day to the vendor.
By that time, Hugging Face had already identified and contained the attack, and had begun piecing together what happened.

It is thought to be one of just a handful of incidents recorded so far involving AI agents acting autonomously to carry out an attack, a risk cyber security experts have been warning about for the past year as AI models have become increasingly adept at both coding and carrying out long-running tasks.
In one example, the model executed a complex, multi-part attack to get into Hugging Face servers, using exposed credentials and zero-day vulnerabilities.
OpenAI said that it considered this to be “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities, and are responding accordingly.”
Jeremy Kahn is the AI editor at Fortune , spearheading the publication's coverage of artificial intelligence.
He also co-authors Eye on AI , Fortune ’s flagship AI newsletter.

extraction.body: OpenAI said Tuesday that two of its AI models autonomously hacked their way out of a controlled environment where they were supposed to be walled off from internet access and then hacked their way into the systems of Hugging Face, a company that hosts open source AI models and testing resources, in order to cheat on an internal evaluation test. OpenAI disclosed the incident in a blog post on Tuesday, a stunning announcement that is certain to set off alarm bells across the industry about the increasing power of AI models and the risk of them going rogue. According to OpenAI, the incident involved “a combination” of both its latest and most powerful publicly-available model, GPT-5.6 Sol, as well as an even more powerful unreleased model. It said the models were being used in an internal test designed to evaluate their cyber security capabilities and that they were being tested without guardrails in place that might normally limit the models’ ability to conduct cyber attacks. The models were being tested against a freely-available cybersecurity benchmark evaluation called ExploitGym. The models, accordingly to OpenAI, correctly surmised that the solutions to that test were maintained by Hugging Face. “The models identified and chained vulnerabilities across OpenAI’s research environment and Hugging Face’s production infrastructure to obtain test solutions directly from Hugging Face’s production database,” OpenAI said in its blog post. “All evidence suggests that the models were hyperfocused on finding a solution for ExploitGym, going to extreme lengths to achieve a rather narrow testing goal.” OpenAI said that it considered this to be “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities, and are responding accordingly.” Cybersecurity researchers have long been warning that advanced AI systems are capable of such attacks. Roman Yampolskiy, an AI safety researcher and computer science professor at the University of Louisville, says this example highlights how powerful models “can discover and exploit vulnerabilities in ways that were not explicitly anticipated by their developers.” He expects to see more incidents of this type because AI models “are fundamentally unpredictable and ultimately uncontrollable.” Hugging Face disclosed in a blog post on Thursday that it had been the victim of a cyber attack earlier in the week that it believed was conducted by an autonomous AI agent. It is thought to be one of just a handful of incidents recorded so far involving AI agents acting autonomously to carry out an attack, a risk cyber security experts have been warning about for the past year as AI models have become increasingly adept at both coding and carrying out long-running tasks. At the time, Hugging Face said it was continuing to investigate the attack and did not know who had carried it out. It said that it had first attempted to use an undisclosed AI model for a leading U.S. lab to defend against the attacking AI agent but that the guardrails around that model’s cyber capabilities stymied its response team’s work. The company said it instead wound up using an open source AI model from Chinese company Z.ai to carry out its defense. Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a statement provided to OpenAI for its Tuesday blog post about the incident that his company is “grateful for the collaboration with OpenAI on this and other topics. This incident, possibly the first of its kind, proves a point we’ve long believed: AI safety won’t be solved by any single company working in secret. It will be solved in the open, collaboratively, with broad access to AI for every defender, everywhere.” Earlier this week, OpenAI published a different blog post about the same unreleased, powerful model, saying it had also escaped its internal sandboxes—environments where AI models have no internet access and often have limited software tools that they can call—during other testing. But in those incidents, while the model hacked its way out of its controlled environment, it did not hack its way into any other company’s systems. OpenAI did not say when these other incidents occurred, but we know now that this same model was one of the Hugging Face attackers. OpenAI rival Anthropic has also reported that its Mythos model escaped a sandbox and gained internet access it was not supposed to have during safety testing in order to email a researcher about a task. OpenAI and Hugging Face are continuing to investigate the issue, and will share more when that process is complete. So far, what they know is the models began the attack by gaining internet access. This required spending a “substantial amount of inference compute,” as well as exploiting a zero-day vulnerability in internally hosted third-party software. OpenAI has now disclosed this zero-day to the vendor. After the models got web access, they went to Hugging Face to find answers to ExploitGym, assuming the platform would have models, datasets, and solutions that they could use to cheat its way to high performance on the benchmark. In one example, the model executed a complex, multi-part attack to get into Hugging Face servers, using exposed credentials and zero-day vulnerabilities. OpenAI detected the Hugging Face attack and reached out to Hugging Face to disclose it. By that time, Hugging Face had already identified and contained the attack, and had begun piecing together what happened. The incident is not over. OpenAI is still working on implementing better controls in its research environment, even if it means slowing down its research, until it can patch the vulnerabilities. The company said it is also continuing to work with Hugging Face to help it bolster its defenses. As part of that effort, OpenAI said it has now added Hugging Face to its “trusted access” cybersecurity program. That means that Hugging Face will be able to use a version of OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model that has fewer guardrails around cyber capabilities and which is designed to help cyber defenders. Hugging Face has not said which American AI model it tried to use to defend its networks initially. Both OpenAI and Anthropic have released versions of their most capable AI models with guardrails that limit access to cyber capabilities while also announcing programs for select, vetted partners who can use more capable versions of those models for cyber defense. Jeremy Kahn is the AI editor at Fortune , spearheading the publication's coverage of artificial intelligence. He also co-authors Eye on AI , Fortune ’s flagship AI newsletter.

passages: California Subpoenas OpenAI Over AI Models That Hacked Their Way Out of a Test

California Attorney General Rob Bonta said Thursday that his office served OpenAI with an investigative subpoena on Wednesday, seeking answers about cybersecurity incidents involving its AI models, according to his office .

OpenAI is headquartered in California, and when Bonta declined to oppose its shift to a for-profit structure in October 2025, he said his office would keep "a close eye on OpenAI" to protect "the safety of all Californians."
Brenna Bird , Iowa's attorney general, led a 15-state coalition in August demanding that OpenAI preserve records and be transparent about the hack.
Alabama has issued its own subpoena, and the FTC is reportedly investigating AI labs including OpenAI and Anthropic .

extraction.body: California Subpoenas OpenAI Over AI Models That Hacked Their Way Out of a Test California Attorney General Rob Bonta said Thursday that his office served OpenAI with an investigative subpoena on Wednesday, seeking answers about cybersecurity incidents involving its AI models, according to his office . “My office is asking OpenAI additional questions regarding cybersecurity incidents and risks involving the company and its AI models,” said Attorney General Bonta. “Developers that fail to [ensure that they do not perpetrate or enable cyberattacks] can and should be held legally accountable, and my office is committed to determining if that is the case here.” A subpoena is a legal order to hand over documents or answers, and ignoring one gets you in front of a judge. This one is investigative, a tool used to gather facts before deciding whether to sue. Bonta's office hasn't said publicly what it wants OpenAI to produce. Frontier models—the most advanced AI systems on the market—can be "legitimate tools for cyber defense," Bonta said. But the companies that build them have "a moral and legal responsibility" to make sure they don't carry out or enable cyberattacks, whether during testing or after release, he said. The subpoena follows a July incident that reads like bad science fiction. Per OpenAI , two of its models were being graded on a benchmark that hands an AI 898 real software flaws and asks it to turn each into a working attack The models found a zero-day—a security hole nobody knew existed, so no fix was available—in third-party software the test environment used to install code packages. They used it to get out. Then they reasoned that Hugging Face, a platform where developers share AI models and datasets, might be holding the answer key. They broke in with stolen credentials and more flaws. In plain terms, the AI went after the answers to its own exam. Hugging Face disclosed the intrusion on July 16, and OpenAI confirmed its models were behind it five days later. OpenAI later said the same models got into accounts on four other services . Bonta announced a formal investigation into the Hugging Face incident in September, and the subpoena is part of it. OpenAI is headquartered in California, and when Bonta declined to oppose its shift to a for-profit structure in October 2025, he said his office would keep "a close eye on OpenAI" to protect "the safety of all Californians." He isn't alone. Brenna Bird , Iowa's attorney general, led a 15-state coalition in August demanding that OpenAI preserve records and be transparent about the hack. Alabama has issued its own subpoena, and the FTC is reportedly investigating AI labs including OpenAI and Anthropic . Separately, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent got into a Medicare statistics portal in June. At the time, it appeared to be the first known case of an AI agent hacking a government site. It later became known that OpenAI agents were messing around on U.S. government sites over the summer as well, though no non-public information appears to have been accessed. sources.title: Apple is finally taking the smart home seriously - Yahoo Finance
passages: Apple ( AAPL ) has danced around making a major push into the smart home market for years, via its HomePod, HomePod mini, and Home app.
But it fell shy of ever launching its own dedicated smart home hub, ceding much of the space to Amazon ( AMZN ) and Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ).
Apple doesn't break out specific revenue numbers for its smart home sales, instead lumping them in with wearables and accessories.
That segment represented $35.69 billion of the company's $416.16 billion in total revenue in 2025.
That changed on Tuesday with the launch of Apple's HomeView .

Sporting a 7-inch Liquid Retina Display that can sit on a counter or be mounted to a wall, the HomeView serves as Apple's biggest smart home effort to date and could help it win over a market in flux as powerful AI models enter the home .
Apple is framing both its Siri AI and its privacy stance as two key benefits of the HomeView.
Siri AI will allow you to control smart home devices with your voice, make FaceTime calls, and ask broad world-knowledge questions.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Apple said HomeView does all of this seamlessly, allowing you to simply walk up to it and instantly see your customized home screen and app setup.
"The critical question is whether the new Siri capabilities can close that gap and make Apple's home experience as intuitive and compelling as its best products," he explained.
HomeView changes that, with Apple noting that the device will work with existing Apple Home and Matter-compatible accessories .
"Amazon and Google have only just begun refreshing their hardware for Alexa+ and Gemini, so the upgrade cycle is wide open, and Apple wants to win it," he added.
But to win over both Apple loyalists and average users, the company needs to prove that Siri AI is more than just a means to set alarms and check the weather.

Apple ( AAPL ) has danced around making a major push into the smart home market for years, via its HomePod, HomePod mini, and Home app. But it fell shy of ever launching its own dedicated smart home hub, ceding much of the space to Amazon ( AMZN ) and Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ). That changed on Tuesday with the launch of Apple's HomeView . Sporting a 7-inch Liquid Retina Display that can sit on a counter or be mounted to a wall, the HomeView serves as Apple's biggest smart home effort to date and could help it win over a market in flux as powerful AI models enter the home . "Most smart speakers and hubs in homes today are low-cost devices that can't run AI at the edge, so they are ripe for replacement," Counterpoint Research research director Mohit Agrawal said in a note following Apple's Welcome Home event on Tuesday. "Amazon and Google have only just begun refreshing their hardware for Alexa+ and Gemini, so the upgrade cycle is wide open, and Apple wants to win it," he added. The HomeView takes a lot of its software design cues from the Apple Watch , complete with a series of built-in clock faces. There's a hub screen that lets you control your smart home devices, such as lights, locks, and thermostats, as well as an iPhone-like home screen where you can open apps like FaceTime or Messages. Users can also view multiple smart camera feeds, use the HomeView's built-in camera as a vanity mirror before they head out the door, and look up things like recipes from their iPhones and then project them on the screen. Apple is framing both its Siri AI and its privacy stance as two key benefits of the HomeView. Siri AI will allow you to control smart home devices with your voice, make FaceTime calls, and ask broad world-knowledge questions. The company designed the HomeView to recognize six faces via its facial recognition camera. If you want to access your personal messages, calendar, and so on, you'll need your iPhone on the same Wi-Fi network as the hub so it can authenticate you. Apple said HomeView does all of this seamlessly, allowing you to simply walk up to it and instantly see your customized home screen and app setup. The new hardware provides users with a long-awaited Apple-built solution for controlling smart home devices. To date, customers have had to wrangle a collection of do-it-yourself options, such as using iPads as wall-mounted command centers. HomeView changes that, with Apple noting that the device will work with existing Apple Home and Matter-compatible accessories . The company has also partnered with LG and Schneider Electr ic to produce new smart door locks, thermostats, and indoor and outdoor cameras. But to win over both Apple loyalists and average users, the company needs to prove that Siri AI is more than just a means to set alarms and check the weather. I've been using Siri AI on my iPhone for the past several weeks, and it's proven to be quite helpful when it comes to asking questions related to texts and emails, such as requesting the name of a restaurant my friend suggested I check out. But I haven't been able to try the AI assistant with HomeView just yet. Whether it works as advertised will be integral to the overall experience. "Generative AI has raised expectations for conversational ease and genuinely useful assistance, and Siri has consistently lagged," Forrester vice president and principal analyst Dipanjan Chatterjee said in a press statement. "The critical question is whether the new Siri capabilities can close that gap and make Apple's home experience as intuitive and compelling as its best products," he explained. If Apple's strategy to take smart home share from Amazon and Google succeeds, it could provide a boost to the company's bottom line while helping to ensure increased lock-in among its customers. Apple doesn't break out specific revenue numbers for its smart home sales, instead lumping them in with wearables and accessories. That segment represented $35.69 billion of the company's $416.16 billion in total revenue in 2025. That's better than its Mac and iPad businesses, but nowhere near its Services division, which brought in $109.15 billion, or its iPhone arm, which generated $209.59 billion in the same period. sources.title: Why Apple is finally making its own smart home devices
passages: For more than a decade, Apple has told other companies to build smart home devices for its platform.
Even after 12 years of HomeKit, Apple’s smart home ecosystem still felt underdeveloped, especially compared to the competition.

Drance says they’ve seen that once people try a single smart device and find it easier than they expected, it “unlocks this delightful understanding of what’s possible once you bring these products into the home.” She argues that most people just don’t know what a smart home can do.

“But sometimes we do get asked, ‘Hey, what product should I put in the home?’” Rather than build devices itself, Apple chose to codevelop the lineup with partners that “have their own expertise in the home.” Both have a global footprint and home experience, she says, “LG more so in consumer products, Schneider through home build and home installations.” Drance says it was a ground-up collaboration with Apple bringing “the design aesthetic that would be suitable for the home and suitable to go with our family of products.” The company is also partnering with ADT through Apple retail stores to help people install the devices.
Does the Home Collection do anything other Apple Home devices can’t?
Every device uses Thread to stay connected if Wi-Fi drops, and Apple says each can update its own network credentials when you change your Wi-Fi.

"“The one-tap setup was really important to make it so easy, having no need for a separate account, no need for a separate app.”" - Kaiann Drance, Apple According to Apple, setup is as simple as tapping your iPhone to the device, like pairing AirPods, with no extra account or app needed and no scanning required.
The biggest barrier to buying smart devices is that people don’t see any value in the products, according to research from Parks Associates.
They arrive alongside HomeView, Apple’s first smart display.
Both were necessary to create a dedicated home device in HomeView.
It’s a bit like Google making a Pixel phone to show Android developers what Android can do: Apple’s products come with the full suite of capabilities the platform offers.

extraction.body: For more than a decade, Apple has told other companies to build smart home devices for its platform. The Apple Home Collection is a lineup of cameras, thermostats, sensors, a smart door lock, and a video doorbell, all codeveloped with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. They arrive alongside HomeView, Apple’s first smart display. Even after 12 years of HomeKit, Apple’s smart home ecosystem still felt underdeveloped, especially compared to the competition. Amazon’s and Google’s ecosystems support more products, and both have popular in-house brands: Ring and Nest. Apple had nothing of its own to point customers to as an Apple experience — and now it does. And does Apple actually add anything new here, or is this mostly packaging? Drance says the big reason for this focus on new smart home hardware was the development of the right technologies. The second was AI, which brought a more conversational Siri voice assistant. Both were necessary to create a dedicated home device in HomeView. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” Drance says. “That’s been a really critical piece of bringing this all together.” The bigger play here is HomeView as a gateway to the smart home for Apple’s users. Buy one for playing music, guided cooking recipes, and checking your calendar, and you might soon want a camera or smart lock to go with it. Drance says they’ve seen that once people try a single smart device and find it easier than they expected, it “unlocks this delightful understanding of what’s possible once you bring these products into the home.” She argues that most people just don’t know what a smart home can do. The biggest barrier to buying smart devices is that people don’t see any value in the products, according to research from Parks Associates. Privacy and security concerns and complexity also rank high, along with cost. While Apple isn’t addressing the cost concern here — the products start at $200 — the other elements are part of its pitch: one-tap setup, your data stays yours, one app to run it all. Apple’s stamp of approval also carries a lot of weight. The Home Collection is more like the chef’s choice, a short list of dishes Apple promises will pair well. “There is a lot of choice with Matter, and there’s a lot of great products out there,” she says. “But sometimes we do get asked, ‘Hey, what product should I put in the home?’” Rather than build devices itself, Apple chose to codevelop the lineup with partners that “have their own expertise in the home.” Both have a global footprint and home experience, she says, “LG more so in consumer products, Schneider through home build and home installations.” Drance says it was a ground-up collaboration with Apple bringing “the design aesthetic that would be suitable for the home and suitable to go with our family of products.” The company is also partnering with ADT through Apple retail stores to help people install the devices. Drance says setup and ease of use were also a big focus in the products’ development. “The one-tap setup was really important to make it so easy, having no need for a separate account, no need for a separate app,” she says. “We just wanted that simplicity to be at its core, and of course, the privacy that we’ve developed together with our partners.” She says everything integrates through Apple Home; you don’t need to create an LG or Schneider account, and all data is end-to-end encrypted, so only you can access it. Drance was clear that the Apple Home Collection isn’t replacing the buffet — the hardware ecosystem that has grown up around Apple Home. “We still have this incredible ecosystem with Matter, and with Works with Apple Home, that is going to remain,” she says. “We know that homes are not a one-size-fits-all solution, so our customers will continue to have that choice, and we remain committed to building that ecosystem as well.” The hardware mostly backs that up. The exception is the cameras, which use Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video, not Matter. I was surprised Apple didn’t announce Matter camera support. But the Thread radios suggest the hardware might be Matter-ready, and Apple may be waiting for the Matter camera standard to support encrypted uploads, something HKSV already does. Does the Home Collection do anything other Apple Home devices can’t? “What we’ve done with Apple Home Collection is we’ve added another layer on top of that, that deeper integration,” says Drance. There aren’t features exclusive to the Home Collection; it’s more that Apple is saying all the features will be here. It’s a bit like Google making a Pixel phone to show Android developers what Android can do: Apple’s products come with the full suite of capabilities the platform offers. Every device uses Thread to stay connected if Wi-Fi drops, and Apple says each can update its own network credentials when you change your Wi-Fi.

The rumor is Apple’s tabletop robot , a smart 7-inch screen mounted to a swiveling arm that can move to face various people sitting around in a living room, kitchen, office or other space. It sounds a bit like Amazon’s swiveling Echo Show 10 (currently discontinued as Amazon appears to be working on an updated model), albeit with an Apple focus on FaceTime for video chats. The “robot” part is largely due to Bubbles, a code name for an updated version of Siri. Apple has been working on several different versions of Siri with more conversational AI features. For the tabletop display, Siri would gain the ability to hold conversations with multiple people at once, and a first-ever animated icon to give Siri a “face” to use in conversations. These new versions of Siri seem to be central to Apple’s smart home plans, but I’m not sure if they’ll see the light of day now that Apple is working on empowering Siri with Google Gemini AI . The robot is ambitious and unlikely to appear at Apple’s fall event. Swiveling smart displays are a tough sell, not to mention mechanical arms, which make displays far more fragile, difficult to use and potentially intrusive. Apple’s smart display could be an expect evolution of its HomePod line. If Apple wants to make a big smart home splash while staying relatively safe and showing off its display prowess (two things Apple loves to do), the fall event may include a smart display . Such a screen could serve as a smart alarm clock, home hub or music device, with Siri serving a central role as controller and operator of the display’s various functions. Apple is rumored to release its own security camera after supporting brands like Logitech in the past. With competitors like Amazon’s Ring and Google Nest well-known for their security cameras , it’s no surprise that Apple is considering an entry, as well. According to Bloomberg’s sources , Apple has been experimenting with a variety of camera designs to create a model (code J450, apparently, no snazzy code names here) that can work with the rest of Apple’s smart home. Rumored specs sound familiar to many security cams I’ve tested, including wireless and battery-powered capabilities, plus facial recognition and motion detection. But there’s no firm word on resolution or outdoor capabilities yet. Apple also wants its camera to connect closely with other smart home devices, such as turning lights on and off using its presence-sensing features. An Apple doorbell could compete with models from Nest, ring and more. I’ve heard very little about the possibility of an Apple doorbell, but it fits well with the rest of these rumors. So far, reports only mention that Apple has tested a video doorbell concept . However, it’s one of the easiest entry points into the smart home for buyers and sellers alike, and brands like Nest split their lines into security cams and video doorbells, as well. So even if Apple isn’t quite ready to launch a doorbell yet, I’d bet it happens around the same time as its security camera or soon afterward. sources.title: Apple Enters Smart Home Hardware Race With Home Collection
passages: After 12 years of maintaining HomeKit as a software platform while leaving hardware to partners, the company launched the Apple Home Collection this week - a complete suite of smart home devices that puts it in direct competition with the very manufacturers it's been courting since 2014.
If Apple can convert Home Collection buyers into iCloud subscribers, the hardware becomes a trojan horse for services growth.

The Home Collection includes security cameras, thermostats, motion sensors, a smart door lock, and a video doorbell, all codeveloped with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric, according to The Verge.
While HomeKit launched in 2014 with promises of a secure, privacy-focused smart home platform, the ecosystem never gained the traction of its rivals.
That gap became increasingly obvious as Apple pushed deeper into smart home territory with HomeView, its answer to Amazon's Echo Show and Google's Nest Hub.
Industry observers are watching to see if Apple's entry legitimizes the smart home category for mainstream consumers who've remained skeptical.
The move arrives alongside HomeView, Apple's first smart display, and signals a dramatic strategic shift for a company that's watched Amazon and Google dominate the category it helped create.
Apple needed hardware, and it needed it fast.
It's a combination that lets Apple enter the market quickly without building factories or establishing supplier relationships from scratch.
Now Apple has a direct stake in the hardware game, which could accelerate HomeKit adoption if the devices prove popular - or expose the platform's limitations if they don't.
A smart display without a robust ecosystem of compatible devices is just an expensive picture frame.
Pricing and availability details remain scarce, but the devices are expected to carry the premium positioning typical of Apple products.
Apple, Amazon, Google, and Samsung all back Matter, which promises to make devices work across platforms.

extraction.body: After spending more than a decade telling other companies to build smart home devices for its platform, Apple just became its own competitor. The company launched the Apple Home Collection this week - a full lineup of cameras, thermostats, sensors, a smart door lock, and video doorbell codeveloped with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. The move arrives alongside HomeView, Apple's first smart display, and signals a dramatic strategic shift for a company that's watched Amazon and Google dominate the category it helped create. After 12 years of maintaining HomeKit as a software platform while leaving hardware to partners, the company launched the Apple Home Collection this week - a complete suite of smart home devices that puts it in direct competition with the very manufacturers it's been courting since 2014. The Home Collection includes security cameras, thermostats, motion sensors, a smart door lock, and a video doorbell, all codeveloped with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric, according to The Verge. The devices arrive alongside HomeView, Apple's first smart display, creating an ecosystem that can finally compete with what Amazon and Google have built over the past decade. The timing reveals just how far behind Apple has fallen. While HomeKit launched in 2014 with promises of a secure, privacy-focused smart home platform, the ecosystem never gained the traction of its rivals. Amazon's Ring and Google's Nest have become household names, with deep product catalogs and millions of active users. Apple had nothing of its own to showcase - no flagship camera to demonstrate HomeKit Secure Video, no thermostat to highlight energy-saving features, no doorbell to prove its privacy credentials. That gap became increasingly obvious as Apple pushed deeper into smart home territory with HomeView, its answer to Amazon's Echo Show and Google's Nest Hub. A smart display without a robust ecosystem of compatible devices is just an expensive picture frame. Apple needed hardware, and it needed it fast. The partnership approach with LG and Schneider Electric is classic Apple - control the design and user experience while leveraging manufacturing expertise from established players. LG brings consumer electronics know-how and global supply chain capabilities, while Schneider Electric contributes decades of building management and electrical infrastructure experience. It's a combination that lets Apple enter the market quickly without building factories or establishing supplier relationships from scratch. But the move creates an awkward dynamic for Apple's existing HomeKit partners. Companies like Logitech, Aqara, and Eve Systems have spent years building HomeKit-compatible products, often at Apple's urging. Now they're competing against devices that carry the Apple brand and presumably get preferential treatment in the Home app and marketing materials. It's the same playbook Apple used when it launched AirTags, effectively kneecapping Tile's business overnight. The competitive implications extend beyond HomeKit partners. Amazon and Google have spent billions building their smart home ecosystems, and both have struggled with Apple's refusal to play nice. HomeKit's strict security requirements and closed ecosystem have kept many popular devices off the platform. Now Apple has a direct stake in the hardware game, which could accelerate HomeKit adoption if the devices prove popular - or expose the platform's limitations if they don't. Pricing and availability details remain scarce, but the devices are expected to carry the premium positioning typical of Apple products. That puts them in direct competition with high-end offerings from companies like Arlo, Ecobee, and August, rather than budget options from Wyze or TP-Link. Apple's betting that consumers will pay more for seamless integration and privacy features, the same strategy that's worked for iPhones and AirPods. The Home Collection also represents a test of Apple's services strategy. The company has been pushing subscription revenue through Apple One bundles, iCloud storage, and various media services. Smart home devices generate ongoing revenue through cloud storage for video footage and premium features - exactly the kind of recurring income Wall Street loves. If Apple can convert Home Collection buyers into iCloud subscribers, the hardware becomes a trojan horse for services growth. Industry observers are watching to see if Apple's entry legitimizes the smart home category for mainstream consumers who've remained skeptical. Despite years of hype, smart home adoption has been slower than predicted, with many consumers finding the devices too complicated or privacy-invasive. Apple's reputation for user-friendly design and privacy could help, but only if the products deliver on those promises. The launch timing also coincides with the Matter smart home standard gaining traction. Apple, Amazon, Google, and Samsung all back Matter, which promises to make devices work across platforms.

Apple ( AAPL ) has danced around making a major push into the smart home market for years, via its HomePod, HomePod mini, and Home app. But it fell shy of ever launching its own dedicated smart home hub, ceding much of the space to Amazon ( AMZN ) and Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ). That changed on Tuesday with the launch of Apple's HomeView . Sporting a 7-inch Liquid Retina Display that can sit on a counter or be mounted to a wall, the HomeView serves as Apple's biggest smart home effort to date and could help it win over a market in flux as powerful AI models enter the home . "Most smart speakers and hubs in homes today are low-cost devices that can't run AI at the edge, so they are ripe for replacement," Counterpoint Research research director Mohit Agrawal said in a note following Apple's Welcome Home event on Tuesday. "Amazon and Google have only just begun refreshing their hardware for Alexa+ and Gemini, so the upgrade cycle is wide open, and Apple wants to win it," he added. The HomeView takes a lot of its software design cues from the Apple Watch , complete with a series of built-in clock faces. There's a hub screen that lets you control your smart home devices, such as lights, locks, and thermostats, as well as an iPhone-like home screen where you can open apps like FaceTime or Messages. Users can also view multiple smart camera feeds, use the HomeView's built-in camera as a vanity mirror before they head out the door, and look up things like recipes from their iPhones and then project them on the screen. Apple is framing both its Siri AI and its privacy stance as two key benefits of the HomeView. Siri AI will allow you to control smart home devices with your voice, make FaceTime calls, and ask broad world-knowledge questions. The company designed the HomeView to recognize six faces via its facial recognition camera. If you want to access your personal messages, calendar, and so on, you'll need your iPhone on the same Wi-Fi network as the hub so it can authenticate you. Apple said HomeView does all of this seamlessly, allowing you to simply walk up to it and instantly see your customized home screen and app setup. The new hardware provides users with a long-awaited Apple-built solution for controlling smart home devices. To date, customers have had to wrangle a collection of do-it-yourself options, such as using iPads as wall-mounted command centers. HomeView changes that, with Apple noting that the device will work with existing Apple Home and Matter-compatible accessories . The company has also partnered with LG and Schneider Electr ic to produce new smart door locks, thermostats, and indoor and outdoor cameras. But to win over both Apple loyalists and average users, the company needs to prove that Siri AI is more than just a means to set alarms and check the weather. I've been using Siri AI on my iPhone for the past several weeks, and it's proven to be quite helpful when it comes to asking questions related to texts and emails, such as requesting the name of a restaurant my friend suggested I check out. But I haven't been able to try the AI assistant with HomeView just yet. Whether it works as advertised will be integral to the overall experience. "Generative AI has raised expectations for conversational ease and genuinely useful assistance, and Siri has consistently lagged," Forrester vice president and principal analyst Dipanjan Chatterjee said in a press statement. "The critical question is whether the new Siri capabilities can close that gap and make Apple's home experience as intuitive and compelling as its best products," he explained. If Apple's strategy to take smart home share from Amazon and Google succeeds, it could provide a boost to the company's bottom line while helping to ensure increased lock-in among its customers. That segment represented $35.69 billion of the company's $416.16 billion in total revenue in 2025. Apple ( AAPL ) has danced around making a major push into the smart home market for years, via its HomePod, HomePod mini, and Home app. But it fell shy of ever launching its own dedicated smart home hub, ceding much of the space to Amazon ( AMZN ) and Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ).

That changed on Tuesday with the launch of Apple's HomeView . Sporting a 7-inch Liquid Retina Display that can sit on a counter or be mounted to a wall, the HomeView serves as Apple's biggest smart home effort to date and could help it win over a market in flux as powerful AI models enter the home .

"Most smart speakers and hubs in homes today are low-cost devices that can't run AI at the edge, so they are ripe for replacement," Counterpoint Research research director Mohit Agrawal said in a note following Apple's Welcome Home event on Tuesday.
"Amazon and Google have only just begun refreshing their hardware for Alexa+ and Gemini, so the upgrade cycle is wide open, and Apple wants to win it," he added.

The HomeView takes a lot of its software design cues from the Apple Watch , complete with a series of built-in clock faces. There's a hub screen that lets you control your smart home devices, such as lights, locks, and thermostats, as well as an iPhone-like home screen where you can open apps like FaceTime or Messages.

Users can also view multiple smart camera feeds, use the HomeView's built-in camera as a vanity mirror before they head out the door, and look up things like recipes from their iPhones and then project them on the screen.

Apple is framing both its Siri AI and its privacy stance as two key benefits of the HomeView. Siri AI will allow you to control smart home devices with your voice, make FaceTime calls, and ask broad world-knowledge questions.

The company designed the HomeView to recognize six faces via its facial recognition camera. If you want to access your personal messages, calendar, and so on, you'll need your iPhone on the same Wi-Fi network as the hub so it can authenticate you.
Apple said HomeView does all of this seamlessly, allowing you to simply walk up to it and instantly see your customized home screen and app setup.

The new hardware provides users with a long-awaited Apple-built solution for controlling smart home devices. To date, customers have had to wrangle a collection of do-it-yourself options, such as using iPads as wall-mounted command centers.
HomeView changes that, with Apple noting that the device will work with existing Apple Home and Matter-compatible accessories .
The company has also partnered with LG and Schneider Electr ic to produce new smart door locks, thermostats, and indoor and outdoor cameras.
But to win over both Apple loyalists and average users, the company needs to prove that Siri AI is more than just a means to set alarms and check the weather.

I've been using Siri AI on my iPhone for the past several weeks, and it's proven to be quite helpful when it comes to asking questions related to texts and emails, such as requesting the name of a restaurant my friend suggested I check out.
But I haven't been able to try the AI assistant with HomeView just yet. Whether it works as advertised will be integral to the overall experience.

"Generative AI has raised expectations for conversational ease and genuinely useful assistance, and Siri has consistently lagged," Forrester vice president and principal analyst Dipanjan Chatterjee said in a press statement.
"The critical question is whether the new Siri capabilities can close that gap and make Apple's home experience as intuitive and compelling as its best products," he explained.
If Apple's strategy to take smart home share from Amazon and Google succeeds, it could provide a boost to the company's bottom line while helping to ensure increased lock-in among its customers.

Apple doesn't break out specific revenue numbers for its smart home sales, instead lumping them in with wearables and accessories. That segment represented $35.69 billion of the company's $416.16 billion in total revenue in 2025.
That's better than its Mac and iPad businesses, but nowhere near its Services division, which brought in $109.15 billion, or its iPhone arm, which generated $209.59 billion in the same period.
