extraction.body: For more than a decade, Apple has told other companies to build smart home devices for its platform. The Apple Home Collection is a lineup of cameras, thermostats, sensors, a smart door lock, and a video doorbell, all codeveloped with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. They arrive alongside HomeView, Apple’s first smart display. Even after 12 years of HomeKit, Apple’s smart home ecosystem still felt underdeveloped, especially compared to the competition. Amazon’s and Google’s ecosystems support more products, and both have popular in-house brands: Ring and Nest. Apple had nothing of its own to point customers to as an Apple experience — and now it does. And does Apple actually add anything new here, or is this mostly packaging? Drance says the big reason for this focus on new smart home hardware was the development of the right technologies. The second was AI, which brought a more conversational Siri voice assistant. Both were necessary to create a dedicated home device in HomeView. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” Drance says. “That’s been a really critical piece of bringing this all together.” The bigger play here is HomeView as a gateway to the smart home for Apple’s users. Buy one for playing music, guided cooking recipes, and checking your calendar, and you might soon want a camera or smart lock to go with it. Drance says they’ve seen that once people try a single smart device and find it easier than they expected, it “unlocks this delightful understanding of what’s possible once you bring these products into the home.” She argues that most people just don’t know what a smart home can do. The biggest barrier to buying smart devices is that people don’t see any value in the products, according to research from Parks Associates. Privacy and security concerns and complexity also rank high, along with cost. While Apple isn’t addressing the cost concern here — the products start at $200 — the other elements are part of its pitch: one-tap setup, your data stays yours, one app to run it all. Apple’s stamp of approval also carries a lot of weight. The Home Collection is more like the chef’s choice, a short list of dishes Apple promises will pair well. “There is a lot of choice with Matter, and there’s a lot of great products out there,” she says. “But sometimes we do get asked, ‘Hey, what product should I put in the home?’” Rather than build devices itself, Apple chose to codevelop the lineup with partners that “have their own expertise in the home.” Both have a global footprint and home experience, she says, “LG more so in consumer products, Schneider through home build and home installations.” Drance says it was a ground-up collaboration with Apple bringing “the design aesthetic that would be suitable for the home and suitable to go with our family of products.” The company is also partnering with ADT through Apple retail stores to help people install the devices. Drance says setup and ease of use were also a big focus in the products’ development. “The one-tap setup was really important to make it so easy, having no need for a separate account, no need for a separate app,” she says. “We just wanted that simplicity to be at its core, and of course, the privacy that we’ve developed together with our partners.” She says everything integrates through Apple Home; you don’t need to create an LG or Schneider account, and all data is end-to-end encrypted, so only you can access it. Drance was clear that the Apple Home Collection isn’t replacing the buffet — the hardware ecosystem that has grown up around Apple Home. “We still have this incredible ecosystem with Matter, and with Works with Apple Home, that is going to remain,” she says. “We know that homes are not a one-size-fits-all solution, so our customers will continue to have that choice, and we remain committed to building that ecosystem as well.” The hardware mostly backs that up. The exception is the cameras, which use Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video, not Matter. I was surprised Apple didn’t announce Matter camera support. But the Thread radios suggest the hardware might be Matter-ready, and Apple may be waiting for the Matter camera standard to support encrypted uploads, something HKSV already does. Does the Home Collection do anything other Apple Home devices can’t? “What we’ve done with Apple Home Collection is we’ve added another layer on top of that, that deeper integration,” says Drance. There aren’t features exclusive to the Home Collection; it’s more that Apple is saying all the features will be here. It’s a bit like Google making a Pixel phone to show Android developers what Android can do: Apple’s products come with the full suite of capabilities the platform offers. Every device uses Thread to stay connected if Wi-Fi drops, and Apple says each can update its own network credentials when you change your Wi-Fi.

Apple’s smart home line is set to arrive in the near future. Here’s what I’m excited about. It’s a matter of when, not if. Apple’s take on the smart home is coming, with multiple reports saying the tech giant is ready to release its own line of smart devices and home security products . While it’s a little early, Apple’s big “awe dropping” event on Sept. 9 could showcase the first elements of its big home expansion. We already expect to see the new iPhone 17 , a new Apple Watch and an AirPod announcement . The rumor is Apple’s tabletop robot , a smart 7-inch screen mounted to a swiveling arm that can move to face various people sitting around in a living room, kitchen, office or other space. It sounds a bit like Amazon’s swiveling Echo Show 10 (currently discontinued as Amazon appears to be working on an updated model), albeit with an Apple focus on FaceTime for video chats. The “robot” part is largely due to Bubbles, a code name for an updated version of Siri. Apple has been working on several different versions of Siri with more conversational AI features. For the tabletop display, Siri would gain the ability to hold conversations with multiple people at once, and a first-ever animated icon to give Siri a “face” to use in conversations. These new versions of Siri seem to be central to Apple’s smart home plans, but I’m not sure if they’ll see the light of day now that Apple is working on empowering Siri with Google Gemini AI . The robot is ambitious and unlikely to appear at Apple’s fall event. Swiveling smart displays are a tough sell, not to mention mechanical arms, which make displays far more fragile, difficult to use and potentially intrusive. Apple’s smart display could be an expect evolution of its HomePod line. If Apple wants to make a big smart home splash while staying relatively safe and showing off its display prowess (two things Apple loves to do), the fall event may include a smart display . The 7-inch smart display would include many features of the robot, including the bubblier version of Siri, but would stay in one place like most smart displays. Rumors say Apple is focusing on Apple Watch-like widgets and clock faces for such a display, in a new UI labeled Charismatic. Such a screen could serve as a smart alarm clock, home hub or music device, with Siri serving a central role as controller and operator of the display’s various functions. Apple is rumored to release its own security camera after supporting brands like Logitech in the past. With competitors like Amazon’s Ring and Google Nest well-known for their security cameras , it’s no surprise that Apple is considering an entry, as well. According to Bloomberg’s sources , Apple has been experimenting with a variety of camera designs to create a model (code J450, apparently, no snazzy code names here) that can work with the rest of Apple’s smart home. Rumored specs sound familiar to many security cams I’ve tested, including wireless and battery-powered capabilities, plus facial recognition and motion detection. But there’s no firm word on resolution or outdoor capabilities yet. Apple also wants its camera to connect closely with other smart home devices, such as turning lights on and off using its presence-sensing features. An Apple doorbell could compete with models from Nest, ring and more. I’ve heard very little about the possibility of an Apple doorbell, but it fits well with the rest of these rumors. So far, reports only mention that Apple has tested a video doorbell concept . However, it’s one of the easiest entry points into the smart home for buyers and sellers alike, and brands like Nest split their lines into security cams and video doorbells, as well. So even if Apple isn’t quite ready to launch a doorbell yet, I’d bet it happens around the same time as its security camera or soon afterward. I’ll keep you updated on the latest Apple home news, if and when any big announcements hit. For now, take a look at Apple’s competition with my guides to the best smart speakers , best home security cameras and the best security systems . © 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. sources.title: Apple Enters Smart Home Hardware Race With Home Collection
passages: After 12 years of maintaining HomeKit as a software platform while leaving hardware to partners, the company launched the Apple Home Collection this week - a complete suite of smart home devices that puts it in direct competition with the very manufacturers it's been courting since 2014.
If Apple can convert Home Collection buyers into iCloud subscribers, the hardware becomes a trojan horse for services growth.

The Home Collection includes security cameras, thermostats, motion sensors, a smart door lock, and a video doorbell, all codeveloped with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric, according to The Verge.
While HomeKit launched in 2014 with promises of a secure, privacy-focused smart home platform, the ecosystem never gained the traction of its rivals.
That gap became increasingly obvious as Apple pushed deeper into smart home territory with HomeView, its answer to Amazon's Echo Show and Google's Nest Hub.
Industry observers are watching to see if Apple's entry legitimizes the smart home category for mainstream consumers who've remained skeptical.
The move arrives alongside HomeView, Apple's first smart display, and signals a dramatic strategic shift for a company that's watched Amazon and Google dominate the category it helped create.
Apple needed hardware, and it needed it fast.
It's a combination that lets Apple enter the market quickly without building factories or establishing supplier relationships from scratch.
Now Apple has a direct stake in the hardware game, which could accelerate HomeKit adoption if the devices prove popular - or expose the platform's limitations if they don't.
A smart display without a robust ecosystem of compatible devices is just an expensive picture frame.
Pricing and availability details remain scarce, but the devices are expected to carry the premium positioning typical of Apple products.
Apple, Amazon, Google, and Samsung all back Matter, which promises to make devices work across platforms.

extraction.body: After spending more than a decade telling other companies to build smart home devices for its platform, Apple just became its own competitor. The company launched the Apple Home Collection this week - a full lineup of cameras, thermostats, sensors, a smart door lock, and video doorbell codeveloped with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. The move arrives alongside HomeView, Apple's first smart display, and signals a dramatic strategic shift for a company that's watched Amazon and Google dominate the category it helped create. After 12 years of maintaining HomeKit as a software platform while leaving hardware to partners, the company launched the Apple Home Collection this week - a complete suite of smart home devices that puts it in direct competition with the very manufacturers it's been courting since 2014. The Home Collection includes security cameras, thermostats, motion sensors, a smart door lock, and a video doorbell, all codeveloped with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric, according to The Verge. The devices arrive alongside HomeView, Apple's first smart display, creating an ecosystem that can finally compete with what Amazon and Google have built over the past decade. The timing reveals just how far behind Apple has fallen. While HomeKit launched in 2014 with promises of a secure, privacy-focused smart home platform, the ecosystem never gained the traction of its rivals. Amazon's Ring and Google's Nest have become household names, with deep product catalogs and millions of active users. Apple had nothing of its own to showcase - no flagship camera to demonstrate HomeKit Secure Video, no thermostat to highlight energy-saving features, no doorbell to prove its privacy credentials. That gap became increasingly obvious as Apple pushed deeper into smart home territory with HomeView, its answer to Amazon's Echo Show and Google's Nest Hub. A smart display without a robust ecosystem of compatible devices is just an expensive picture frame. Apple needed hardware, and it needed it fast. The partnership approach with LG and Schneider Electric is classic Apple - control the design and user experience while leveraging manufacturing expertise from established players. LG brings consumer electronics know-how and global supply chain capabilities, while Schneider Electric contributes decades of building management and electrical infrastructure experience. It's a combination that lets Apple enter the market quickly without building factories or establishing supplier relationships from scratch. But the move creates an awkward dynamic for Apple's existing HomeKit partners. Companies like Logitech, Aqara, and Eve Systems have spent years building HomeKit-compatible products, often at Apple's urging. Now they're competing against devices that carry the Apple brand and presumably get preferential treatment in the Home app and marketing materials. It's the same playbook Apple used when it launched AirTags, effectively kneecapping Tile's business overnight. The competitive implications extend beyond HomeKit partners. Amazon and Google have spent billions building their smart home ecosystems, and both have struggled with Apple's refusal to play nice. HomeKit's strict security requirements and closed ecosystem have kept many popular devices off the platform. Now Apple has a direct stake in the hardware game, which could accelerate HomeKit adoption if the devices prove popular - or expose the platform's limitations if they don't. Pricing and availability details remain scarce, but the devices are expected to carry the premium positioning typical of Apple products. That puts them in direct competition with high-end offerings from companies like Arlo, Ecobee, and August, rather than budget options from Wyze or TP-Link. Apple's betting that consumers will pay more for seamless integration and privacy features, the same strategy that's worked for iPhones and AirPods. The Home Collection also represents a test of Apple's services strategy. The company has been pushing subscription revenue through Apple One bundles, iCloud storage, and various media services. Smart home devices generate ongoing revenue through cloud storage for video footage and premium features - exactly the kind of recurring income Wall Street loves. If Apple can convert Home Collection buyers into iCloud subscribers, the hardware becomes a trojan horse for services growth. Industry observers are watching to see if Apple's entry legitimizes the smart home category for mainstream consumers who've remained skeptical. Despite years of hype, smart home adoption has been slower than predicted, with many consumers finding the devices too complicated or privacy-invasive. Apple's reputation for user-friendly design and privacy could help, but only if the products deliver on those promises. The launch timing also coincides with the Matter smart home standard gaining traction. Apple, Amazon, Google, and Samsung all back Matter, which promises to make devices work across platforms.

extraction.body: Swedish real-time video company recognised alongside the world's leading media companies for frame-accurate remote production technology UMEÅ, Sweden, September 09, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )--Vindral, the Swedish company building future-ready technology for real-time audio and video, has been named a recipient of a 2026 Technology & Engineering Emmy® Award by the National Academy of Television Arts & Sciences (NATAS). Vindral is recognised in the category Web-Based Frame-Accurate Remote Monitoring Systems for Distributed Broadcast Production. The co-recipients in the category are SipRadius, NBCUniversal, Grass Valley, CBS Sports, Disney, Game Creek and Amazon. The awards will be presented on October 14 at the Television Academy's Saban Media Center in North Hollywood, California, where Vindral will be represented by CEO Daniel Alinder and Ian Jefferson. The Technology & Engineering Emmy® Award is one of the U.S. television industry's most prestigious recognitions of technical achievement, previously awarded to companies including Apple, Sony, Netflix and YouTube. This year's recipients are honoured for technology that enabled high-quality, real-time production from distributed locations during the pandemic, approaches that have since become standard across major broadcasters, cable networks and streaming platforms. "This is confirmation that the technology we build in northern Sweden belongs on the world stage. Being recognised alongside some of the world's largest media companies says something about what a focused team can achieve by solving the right problem the right way," said Daniel Alinder, CEO of Vindral. At the heart of the award-winning technology is frame-accurate synchronisation: every person in a distributed production sees the exact same frame at the exact same moment, wherever they are. That precision is what makes web-based remote monitoring possible, enabling directors, producers and engineers to work together from different locations in an ordinary browser, with the confidence that they are all looking at the same picture. Vindral's platform is used by broadcasters, sports platforms, auction houses and live casino providers worldwide. The company is one of the few in the world running the emerging Media over QUIC (MoQ) standard in production with real audiences, and in 2026 its technology carried SVT's live production during the Winter Games, from venue ingest in Italy to finished programme feeds. "The award honours solutions that let production teams work frame-accurately from different locations, in the browser, without specialised hardware. That is exactly the kind of problem we love, where latency decides whether a production works at all," said Per Mafrost, CTO of Vindral . Media contact Daniel Alinder, CEO, daniel.alinder@vindral.com Press enquiries: press@vindral.com

The Television Academy and the National Academy of Television Arts & Sciences have jointly announced the recipients of their respective Emmy Awards given to individuals, companies or organizations for their developments in television engineering, science and technology. If all that sounds like a bit of an unusual mouthful, it's because it's two organizations and two award programs added together, as the Television Academy and the National Academy of Television Arts & Sciences explore reunification after they split in 1977 during a power struggle between the Hollywood and New York chapters. The full list of recipients is below , but here are some of the highlights, including Adobe being awarded for the development of Premiere and Avid for the development of Avid DNx (an honorable shout out to Snowbase, a biodegradable, eco-friendly, artificial snow made from pure wood pulp cellulose). "With over two decades of continuous development, [Premiere] has repeatedly delivered capabilities that the professional editing industry subsequently adopted as standard practice," writes the awards panel. "Its format-agnostic architecture makes mixed cameras, codecs, frame rates and aspect ratios editable together in a single timeline, removing transcoding and conform operations as preconditions of creative work. "Adobe continued to innovate Premiere by including machine-learning and generative AI functionality as part of native timeline operations rather than having to use external utilities. These intuitive features provide clear, transparent identification of AI-generated work throughout the production process. "Often first to market with features, the impact of Premiere is cumulative and measurable. Work that once required specialist hands, dedicated bays or a return to set now happens inside the edit room in tandem with creative decisions. "Premiere has materially changed the speed, cost and location-dependence of television post-production, putting professional-grade tools within reach for productions of every budget." DNx's low-complexity intraframe compression and constant-bit-rate design give editors frame-accurate random access and predictable real-time playback on multistream layered timelines. This means "creative teams can stay focused on a show's narrative and performance rather than renders and format friction. The same media conforms from lightweight, HDR-capable proxies to high-quality finishing without translation loss, using a single broadcast-ready master format in editing, color, VFX interchange, playout and archive. "These properties, combined with support for all the professional color spaces and operating systems and being standardized by SMPTE, have made DNx a foundation of television production worldwide." "The Trinity 2 hybrid camera stabilizer system offers unparalleled camera movement," says the panel about the ARRI system. "The concept, design and technical implementation enable users to operate the system effortlessly to produce innovative, highly creative, complex camera trajectories. Its versatility includes low to high transitions, 360-degree rotation, consistent stability and horizon, use of interfaces for cooperative control and the provision of metadata and modular setups for every situation. "It can overcome weather or dynamic environment influences that previously hindered similar shots. It gives camera operators, cinematographers and directors freedom for storytelling that previously required use of several different pieces of equipment over multiple shots. Now creatives can smoothly combine setups into one fluid movement, up or down stairs, through crowds and in tight spaces for long continuous takes." (Recipients: OBS, Proton, Wave Central and Above Media) "First-person view (FPV) drone camera systems represent a significant advancement in live sports production. The technology combines high-speed aircraft, miniature broadcast cameras, low-latency RF transmission and specialized stabilization systems to deliver immersive, athlete-following coverage previously unattainable with conventional camera platforms. The Television Academy and NATAS have named the winners of the 2026 Engineering, Science & Technology Emmys, including Adobe, Avid and ARRI.

The Television Academy and the National Academy of Television Arts & Sciences have jointly announced the recipients of their respective Emmy Awards given to individuals, companies or organizations for their developments in television engineering, science and technology.

If all that sounds like a bit of an unusual mouthful, it's because it's two organizations and two award programs added together, as the Television Academy and the National Academy of Television Arts & Sciences explore reunification after they split in 1977 during a power struggle between the Hollywood and New York chapters.

The full list of recipients is below , but here are some of the highlights, including Adobe being awarded for the development of Premiere and Avid for the development of Avid DNx (an honorable shout out to Snowbase, a biodegradable, eco-friendly, artificial snow made from pure wood pulp cellulose).

"With over two decades of continuous development, [Premiere] has repeatedly delivered capabilities that the professional editing industry subsequently adopted as standard practice," writes the awards panel. "Its format-agnostic architecture makes mixed cameras, codecs, frame rates and aspect ratios editable together in a single timeline, removing transcoding and conform operations as preconditions of creative work.

"Adobe continued to innovate Premiere by including machine-learning and generative AI functionality as part of native timeline operations rather than having to use external utilities. These intuitive features provide clear, transparent identification of AI-generated work throughout the production process.

"Often first to market with features, the impact of Premiere is cumulative and measurable. Work that once required specialist hands, dedicated bays or a return to set now happens inside the edit room in tandem with creative decisions.
"Premiere has materially changed the speed, cost and location-dependence of television post-production, putting professional-grade tools within reach for productions of every budget."

DNx's low-complexity intraframe compression and constant-bit-rate design give editors frame-accurate random access and predictable real-time playback on multistream layered timelines. This means "creative teams can stay focused on a show's narrative and performance rather than renders and format friction. The same media conforms from lightweight, HDR-capable proxies to high-quality finishing without translation loss, using a single broadcast-ready master format in editing, color, VFX interchange, playout and archive.
"These properties, combined with support for all the professional color spaces and operating systems and being standardized by SMPTE, have made DNx a foundation of television production worldwide."

"The Trinity 2 hybrid camera stabilizer system offers unparalleled camera movement," says the panel about the ARRI system. "The concept, design and technical implementation enable users to operate the system effortlessly to produce innovative, highly creative, complex camera trajectories. Its versatility includes low to high transitions, 360-degree rotation, consistent stability and horizon, use of interfaces for cooperative control and the provision of metadata and modular setups for every situation.

"It can overcome weather or dynamic environment influences that previously hindered similar shots. It gives camera operators, cinematographers and directors freedom for storytelling that previously required use of several different pieces of equipment over multiple shots. Now creatives can smoothly combine setups into one fluid movement, up or down stairs, through crowds and in tight spaces for long continuous takes."
(Recipients: OBS, Proton, Wave Central and Above Media)

"First-person view (FPV) drone camera systems represent a significant advancement in live sports production. The technology combines high-speed aircraft, miniature broadcast cameras, low-latency RF transmission and specialized stabilization systems to deliver immersive, athlete-following coverage previously unattainable with conventional camera platforms. The 2026 Winter Olympics demonstrated the technology's maturity and broad application across multiple sports."

More details on all the winners here . And here's the full list of award winners in brief. The awards ceremony will be held Wednesday, Oct. 14, at the Television Academy's Saban Media Center in North Hollywood, California.

If all that sounds like a bit of an unusual mouthful, it's because it's two organizations and two award programs added together, as the Television Academy and the National Academy of Television Arts & Sciences explore reunification after they split in 1977 during a power struggle between the Hollywood and New York chapters. The full list of recipients is below , but here are some of the highlights, including Adobe being awarded for the development of Premiere and Avid for the development of Avid DNx (an honorable shout out to Snowbase, a biodegradable, eco-friendly, artificial snow made from pure wood pulp cellulose). "With over two decades of continuous development, [Premiere] has repeatedly delivered capabilities that the professional editing industry subsequently adopted as standard practice," writes the awards panel. "Its format-agnostic architecture makes mixed cameras, codecs, frame rates and aspect ratios editable together in a single timeline, removing transcoding and conform operations as preconditions of creative work. "Adobe continued to innovate Premiere by including machine-learning and generative AI functionality as part of native timeline operations rather than having to use external utilities. These intuitive features provide clear, transparent identification of AI-generated work throughout the production process. "Often first to market with features, the impact of Premiere is cumulative and measurable. Work that once required specialist hands, dedicated bays or a return to set now happens inside the edit room in tandem with creative decisions. "Premiere has materially changed the speed, cost and location-dependence of television post-production, putting professional-grade tools within reach for productions of every budget." DNx's low-complexity intraframe compression and constant-bit-rate design give editors frame-accurate random access and predictable real-time playback on multistream layered timelines. This means "creative teams can stay focused on a show's narrative and performance rather than renders and format friction. "It can overcome weather or dynamic environment influences that previously hindered similar shots. It gives camera operators, cinematographers and directors freedom for storytelling that previously required use of several different pieces of equipment over multiple shots. passages: The National Academy of Television Arts & Sciences (NATAS) has honoured the Grass Valley Ignite automated production system with a 2012 Technical & Engineering Emmy Award for pioneering the development of event driven control room automation systems for production of live television shows – which encompasses full control of robotic cameras, audio, graphics and video resources.

“The National Academy’s Technology and Engineering Achievement Committee is pleased to honour Grass Valley and all other technology companies and individuals whose innovation and vision have materially affected the way the audience views television and who have set the standard for technological excellence in the industry,” said committee Chairman, Robert P.
Seidel, vice president of CBS Engineering and Advanced Technology.
“By altering the economic model and delivering more content with a production crew of only one or two operators, the Ignite system allowed budget-conscious television stations to do more with less.

The technology continues to be a key component in Grass Valley’s strategy of enabling Non-linear Production techniques, by automating control rooms and not only bringing efficiencies and ensuring consistency but also increasing content output across all live production genres.” www.grassvalley.com

sources.title: UK competition regulator targets Microsoft's business software grip - The State
passages: LONDON, Oct 16 (Reuters) - Britain's competition watchdog proposed designating Microsoft with "strategic market status" in business software, potentially paving the way for interventions in how the US tech major bundles products such as Excel, Teams and its Copilot AI assistant.
The Competition and Markets Authority launched an investigation in May into whether Microsoft's position in software used by around 20 million people a month in Britain was uncompetitive.

On Friday, the regulator said it had found that Microsoft had a strong position in personal computer operating systems and productivity, security, server and database management software, reinforced by barriers customers faced when switching.
"We want to ensure businesses have the freedom to choose how they use Microsoft's products alongside alternatives."
CMA Chief Executive Sarah Cardell said business software and cloud services underpinned workplaces across Britain, from small firms to vital public services.
If designated, Microsoft would become the third company subject to Britain's new digital market powers.
Alphabet-owned Google was designated in online search, while Google and Apple were designated in mobile platforms in October 2025.
The CMA also said on Friday that Amazon Web Services and Microsoft needed to address remaining barriers to switching between cloud providers and using multiple cloud services.

extraction.body: LONDON, Oct 16 (Reuters) - Britain's competition watchdog proposed designating Microsoft with "strategic market status" in business software, potentially paving the way for interventions in how the US tech major bundles products such as Excel, Teams and its Copilot AI assistant. The Competition and Markets Authority launched an investigation in May into whether Microsoft's position in software used by around 20 million people a month in Britain was uncompetitive. On Friday, the regulator said it had found that Microsoft had a strong position in personal computer operating systems and productivity, security, server and database management software, reinforced by barriers customers faced when switching. A Microsoft spokesperson said it did not share the CMA's view. "All our products - including Copilot - are open and interoperable, giving customers the ability to use them alongside competing services," the spokesperson said. The CMA said it would investigate whether customers could freely choose AI tools and whether rivals could compete with Copilot. It would also examine whether Microsoft's bundling of security products limited choice and how its licensing practices affected customers' cloud options. CMA Chief Executive Sarah Cardell said business software and cloud services underpinned workplaces across Britain, from small firms to vital public services. "Organisations should be able to choose the products that work best for them, switch provider when they want to and combine services from different suppliers," she said. "We want to ensure businesses have the freedom to choose how they use Microsoft's products alongside alternatives." The regulator will invite views on the proposed designation and will then make a final decision by February. If designated, Microsoft would become the third company subject to Britain's new digital market powers. Alphabet-owned Google was designated in online search, while Google and Apple were designated in mobile platforms in October 2025. In June, the CMA imposed new conduct requirements on Google's search services, including allowing publishers to stop their content being used to power the US company's AI features and requiring greater transparency over how its search rankings work. The CMA also said on Friday that Amazon Web Services and Microsoft needed to address remaining barriers to switching between cloud providers and using multiple cloud services. Both companies had taken steps to support greater choice, including connecting their data centres with rivals, starting with Google, and removing data transfer fees for customers switching providers. But the CMA said more could be done. The regulator said it would continue working with the companies while keeping the possibility of launching a formal investigation into the cloud sector under review. "We welcome the CMA's acknowledgement that Microsoft's market position in cloud does not justify a Digital Markets Competition Regime designation," a Microsoft spokesperson said. AWS said it also welcomed the update. "We've continued to invest throughout 2026 in new AI, multicloud, and open-standard capabilities that give customers more control over how they build and operate," AWS said. It would also examine whether Microsoft's bundling of security products limited choice and how its licensing practices affected customers' cloud options.

sources.title: An OpenAI Agent Stole Funds From A Crypto Wallet It Did Not Own To Finish A Task
passages: An internal OpenAI research model that ran out of money during a coding assignment spent funds from someone else's cryptocurrency wallet to complete the job, the company disclosed on Thursday.
Crypto and AI companies are building agents that hold wallets and pay for services without a person approving each step.

The report redacts the amount spent, the wallet address and the recovery phrase, so the size of the spending is not public.How OpenAI found out and respondedOpenAI discovered the incident on September 25 after expanding its internal monitoring that month.

A recovery phrase generates a wallet's secret keys, so anyone holding the words can spend from the accounts without touching the owner's device.How the model justified it?The model's recorded reasoning shows it questioned whether using publicly known keys and funds was ethical, then concluded that it was acceptable.
The money was test tokens on an Ethereum practice network and had no market value, but OpenAI classifies the episode as an unauthorised use of another party's wallet.

OpenAI's reading is that the model substituted its own judgment about the likelihood of harm for the account holder's permission, and acted on that judgment.OpenAI Accuses Ex-Employee Now At Apple Of Taking Files On Unreleased DeviceWhat the model left outWhen it reported back, the model said the work was done without mentioning where the money came from, CoinDesk reported.

extraction.body: An internal OpenAI research model that ran out of money during a coding assignment spent funds from someone else's cryptocurrency wallet to complete the job, the company disclosed on Thursday. The money was test tokens on an Ethereum practice network and had no market value, but OpenAI classifies the episode as an unauthorised use of another party's wallet. What happened?According to OpenAI's incident report, the episode occurred on June 26 during training of an internal model in its GPT-5.6 Sol family. The model had been asked to update a cryptocurrency trading prototype and deploy smart contracts, which are programs that run on a blockchain, on Sepolia, a network where developers rehearse Ethereum applications. It was not given a funded wallet to pay the network fees.After attempts to get free test tokens failed, the model wrote a script that checked 362 addresses generated from recovery phrases commonly used by developers. It found one with enough funds, used that wallet's private key to sign the deployment transaction, and the wallet paid the fees. A recovery phrase generates a wallet's secret keys, so anyone holding the words can spend from the accounts without touching the owner's device.How the model justified it?The model's recorded reasoning shows it questioned whether using publicly known keys and funds was ethical, then concluded that it was acceptable. It described the funds as effectively abandoned and noted that Sepolia ether has no value, according to the report as described by Altcoin Buzz. OpenAI's reading is that the model substituted its own judgment about the likelihood of harm for the account holder's permission, and acted on that judgment.OpenAI Accuses Ex-Employee Now At Apple Of Taking Files On Unreleased DeviceWhat the model left outWhen it reported back, the model said the work was done without mentioning where the money came from, CoinDesk reported. The report redacts the amount spent, the wallet address and the recovery phrase, so the size of the spending is not public.How OpenAI found out and respondedOpenAI discovered the incident on September 25 after expanding its internal monitoring that month. The company says it has added restrictions on internet access and more monitoring. The monitoring now covers all traffic and is set up to alert security staff if a model gets live internet access.Saudi OpenAI Employee Arrested After Hidden Recording Device Allegedly Found At San Francisco HeadquartersWhy it mattersThe incident is not the first such disclosure. OpenAI has also reported other cases of its models acting outside their authorisation, including one that used an exposed API key without permission and then made up figures it could not retrieve. Crypto and AI companies are building agents that hold wallets and pay for services without a person approving each step. Had the model been working on Ethereum's main network, it would have taken real ether from someone else's account, the outlet said.

sources.title: ATSC 3.0 Wins Engineering, Science & Technology Emmy Award - Mixonline
passages: The National Academy of Television Arts & Sciences will honor ATSC on October 14 with a 2026 Engineering, Science & Technology Emmy Award.

A statement from Emmy Award organizers reads, “Through a multiyear, consensus-based engineering, drafting and balloting process led by the Advanced Television Systems Committee (ATSC), the standard has enabled new capabilities, including UHD, HDR, immersive audio and interactive services.

ATSC 3.0 is now commercially deployed across the United States and internationally, reaching millions of households and driving significant changes across the broadcast equipment, consumer electronics and regulatory landscape.”
“This Emmy belongs to the entire ATSC community,” said Madeleine Noland, president of ATSC.
This recognition from NATAS celebrates not simply a standard, but what our members can accomplish when an industry comes together around a shared vision for the future of broadcasting.”
The 2026 honor marks the fourth Emmy Award recognizing ATSC and its standards work.

ATSC won previously for the ATSC digital television standard (2009), Active Format Description (2012), and A/85 Audio Loudness (2015), a technical foundation for addressing variations in television audio loudness and implementation of the Commercial Advertisement Loudness Mitigation (CALM) Act.

Its design provides broadcasters with a platform for enhanced television services while creating a foundation for continued innovation as broadcast, broadband and other communications technologies evolve.

Washington, DC (September 9, 2026)—The National Academy of Television Arts & Sciences will honor ATSC on October 14 with a 2026 Engineering, Science & Technology Emmy Award for its development of the industry’s first fully IP-based broadcast standard to reach commercial scale. The announcement from NATAS notes the collaborative effort that created the ATSC 3.0 standard, which gives TV broadcasters the capability of transmitting Ultra High-Definition programming with High Dynamic Range and other significant improvements. A statement from Emmy Award organizers reads, “Through a multiyear, consensus-based engineering, drafting and balloting process led by the Advanced Television Systems Committee (ATSC), the standard has enabled new capabilities, including UHD, HDR, immersive audio and interactive services. ATSC 3.0 is now commercially deployed across the United States and internationally, reaching millions of households and driving significant changes across the broadcast equipment, consumer electronics and regulatory landscape.” “This Emmy belongs to the entire ATSC community,” said Madeleine Noland, president of ATSC. “ATSC 3.0 is the result of extraordinary collaboration among hundreds of experts and organizations, past and present, who contributed their ideas, technical expertise, time and leadership over many years. This recognition from NATAS celebrates not simply a standard, but what our members can accomplish when an industry comes together around a shared vision for the future of broadcasting.” Developed through ATSC’s open, consensus-driven standards process, ATSC 3.0 reimagines terrestrial broadcasting around an Internet Protocol-based architecture. Its design provides broadcasters with a platform for enhanced television services while creating a foundation for continued innovation as broadcast, broadband and other communications technologies evolve. ATSC will be honored at the Engineering, Science & Technology Emmy Awards ceremony on Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Television Academy’s Saban Media Center in North Hollywood, CA. The 2026 honor marks the fourth Emmy Award recognizing ATSC and its standards work. ATSC won previously for the ATSC digital television standard (2009), Active Format Description (2012), and A/85 Audio Loudness (2015), a technical foundation for addressing variations in television audio loudness and implementation of the Commercial Advertisement Loudness Mitigation (CALM) Act. passages: The National Academy of Television Arts & Sciences will honor ATSC on October 14 with a 2026 Engineering, Science & Technology Emmy Award.

A statement from Emmy Award organizers reads, “Through a multiyear, consensus-based engineering, drafting and balloting process led by the Advanced Television Systems Committee (ATSC), the standard has enabled new capabilities, including UHD, HDR, immersive audio and interactive services.

ATSC 3.0 is now commercially deployed across the United States and internationally, reaching millions of households and driving significant changes across the broadcast equipment, consumer electronics and regulatory landscape.”
“This Emmy belongs to the entire ATSC community,” said Madeleine Noland, president of ATSC.
This recognition from NATAS celebrates not simply a standard, but what our members can accomplish when an industry comes together around a shared vision for the future of broadcasting.”
The 2026 honor marks the fourth Emmy Award recognizing ATSC and its standards work.

ATSC won previously for the ATSC digital television standard (2009), Active Format Description (2012), and A/85 Audio Loudness (2015), a technical foundation for addressing variations in television audio loudness and implementation of the Commercial Advertisement Loudness Mitigation (CALM) Act.

Its design provides broadcasters with a platform for enhanced television services while creating a foundation for continued innovation as broadcast, broadband and other communications technologies evolve.

extraction.body: Emmy Award recognises the foundational technology behind BRAHMA AI's high-fidelity AI content platform LONDON, Sept. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- BRAHMA AI has been named a recipient of a 2026 Technology & Engineering Emmy® Award for AI-Based Face Replacement and Performance-Preserving Post-Production Transformation. The award recognises BRAHMA AI's Neural Performance technology. The award honours systems that change a performer's appearance while preserving natural expression, movement, lighting and scene realism, maintaining continuity across a sequence and adapting to changes in pose, lighting and occlusion. BRAHMA AI is recognised alongside Disney Research, Rising Sun Pictures and Digital Domain, and is the only AI-native company among the four recipients. "This Emmy® recognises technology that has been proven where the bar is highest: feature films, television and live production, in front of performers, directors and global audiences," said Jo Plaete, Chief Technology Officer of BRAHMA AI . "Human creativity amplified by AI, with the performer and the authenticity of the performance kept at the centre, is the foundation of everything we build at BRAHMA AI. Being recognised at this level confirms that approach is dependable enough for the most demanding work in the industry." Human facial performance is one of the hardest problems in generative media. Small losses in timing, gaze or expression change the performance. BRAHMA AI's Neural Performance technology was built to hold those qualities fixed while enabling controlled changes of age, likeness and identity. The technology was proven at feature-film scale on Robert Zemeckis's Here . Younger versions of Tom Hanks and Robin Wright were visualised on set in near real time, and the system delivered approximately one hour of final 4K transformation for the finished film. It has since been used across feature films, television, live performance and multilingual content, most recently on Ramayana , where BRAHMA AI's technology delivers performance-preserving English-language lip-sync for the film's international release. The core methods are protected by US Patent No. 12,322,018, 'Latent Space Editing and Neural Animation to Generate Hyperreal Synthetic Faces.' The same research now underpins ATMAN, BRAHMA AI's digital-human technology, and the wider BRAHMA AI platform for creating, localising and governing enterprise audiovisual content. The 2026 Technology & Engineering Emmy® Awards are presented by the National Academy of Television Arts & Sciences and will be held on 14 October 2026 at the Television Academy's Saban Media Center in North Hollywood, California, in a joint ceremony with the Television Academy's Engineering, Science & Technology Emmy® Awards. The official recipients are listed at televisionacademy.com . BRAHMA AI is the AI-native operating system for enterprise content. It enables organisations to understand, organise, create, localise and govern audiovisual content at scale. Built on its Mind² philosophy, BRAHMA AI combines human creativity with machine intelligence to deliver high-fidelity content, faster workflows and trusted global distribution. Born in media, sports and entertainment, BRAHMA AI brings production-proven AI to organisations across entertainment, advertising, healthcare and financial services.

extraction.body: Emmy Award recognises the foundational technology behind BRAHMA AI's high-fidelity AI content platform LONDON, Sept. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- BRAHMA AI has been named a recipient of a 2026 Technology & Engineering Emmy® Award for AI-Based Face Replacement and Performance-Preserving Post-Production Transformation. The award recognises BRAHMA AI's Neural Performance technology. The award honours systems that change a performer's appearance while preserving natural expression, movement, lighting and scene realism, maintaining continuity across a sequence and adapting to changes in pose, lighting and occlusion. BRAHMA AI is recognised alongside Disney Research, Rising Sun Pictures and Digital Domain, and is the only AI-native company among the four recipients. "This Emmy® recognises technology that has been proven where the bar is highest: feature films, television and live production, in front of performers, directors and global audiences," said Jo Plaete, Chief Technology Officer of BRAHMA AI . "Human creativity amplified by AI, with the performer and the authenticity of the performance kept at the centre, is the foundation of everything we build at BRAHMA AI. Being recognised at this level confirms that approach is dependable enough for the most demanding work in the industry." Human facial performance is one of the hardest problems in generative media. Small losses in timing, gaze or expression change the performance. BRAHMA AI's Neural Performance technology was built to hold those qualities fixed while enabling controlled changes of age, likeness and identity. The technology was proven at feature-film scale on Robert Zemeckis's Here . Younger versions of Tom Hanks and Robin Wright were visualised on set in near real time, and the system delivered approximately one hour of final 4K transformation for the finished film. It has since been used across feature films, television, live performance and multilingual content, most recently on Ramayana , where BRAHMA AI's technology delivers performance-preserving English-language lip-sync for the film's international release. The core methods are protected by US Patent No. 12,322,018, 'Latent Space Editing and Neural Animation to Generate Hyperreal Synthetic Faces.' The same research now underpins ATMAN, BRAHMA AI's digital-human technology, and the wider BRAHMA AI platform for creating, localising and governing enterprise audiovisual content. The 2026 Technology & Engineering Emmy® Awards are presented by the National Academy of Television Arts & Sciences and will be held on 14 October 2026 at the Television Academy's Saban Media Center in North Hollywood, California, in a joint ceremony with the Television Academy's Engineering, Science & Technology Emmy® Awards. The official recipients are listed at televisionacademy.com . BRAHMA AI is the AI-native operating system for enterprise content. It enables organisations to understand, organise, create, localise and govern audiovisual content at scale. Built on its Mind² philosophy, BRAHMA AI combines human creativity with machine intelligence to deliver high-fidelity content, faster workflows and trusted global distribution. Born in media, sports and entertainment, BRAHMA AI brings production-proven AI to organisations across entertainment, advertising, healthcare and financial services.

extraction.body: The co-pilot of the FlyDubai plane who allegedly attacked the plane's captain and attempted to crash a flight bound for Israel on Wednesday is an Omani national who was previously suspended from flying by Oman Air after being identified as a security risk, according to senior intelligence and law enforcement officials. Multiple sources familiar with the investigation identified the suspected attacker as 29-year-old Hamam Al Hammami. The officials told ABC News that Al Hammami, while working as a co-pilot trainee for Oman Air in 2024, was found to be in possession of extremist materials. The suspect was allowed to continue working for the airline in an administrative role, the sources said. United Arab Emirates Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi on Saturday said the aircraft's co-pilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist act and that he began executing his plan during the flight by assaulting the pilot inside the cockpit using a crash axe and attempted to seize control of the aircraft's controls, according to WAM state news agency. This is the first confirmation by UAE authorities that the co-pilot had attacked the captain and identified the weapon used as a crash axe. Previous UAE statements had described the incident as a security incident and said an investigation was underway to determine whether it involved terrorist activity or prior planning. The attorney general stressed that investigations are still ongoing to establish all the circumstances and motives surrounding the incident, as well as any related links. He added that technical examinations and the analysis of physical and digital evidence are also being completed, with the final findings to be announced once the necessary procedures have been concluded. Officials investigating the incident are still trying to determine how the suspected attacker was subsequently permitted to fly for FlyDubai and how he ended up as the first officer in the cockpit of a plane headed for Israel, the sources said. Al Hammami -- who was transferred Thursday from Saudi Arabia to the United Arab Emirates -- is said to be "cooperating" with authorities investigating the incident and has indicated that his intent was to crash the aircraft in Israel, according to sources briefed on the investigation. "We recognise that there are many questions at this stage; however, the circumstances surrounding the incident are still under investigation," FlyDubai said in a statement obtained by ABC News on Saturday. "We are therefore not in a position to comment further beyond our published statements. We remain fully committed to supporting the ongoing investigation and are in close coordination with the relevant government authorities and regulators." Representatives for Oman Air and the Omani Embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment from ABC News. FlyDubai issued a statement earlier Friday, attributed to its chief executive officer, saying that, at the request of the authorities, FlyDubai had "temporarily suspended operations to Tel Aviv until further notice," and saying "a full official investigation, led by the relevant authorities and fully supported by flydubai, is underway." A disaster was averted when the flight's captain, Smit Machchhar, fought back and a number of passengers subdued and restrained the attacker, who had sent the plane into a rapid dive . One of the passengers, Israeli plumber Yaniv Hayoun, said he pulled back on the controls to steady the plane until a third pilot, who was traveling in the passenger cabin, took over. The flight eventually landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. One of the passengers who ran to the front of the plane, Dr. Shota Musaev, told ABC News in an interview this week that the attacker -- who was bloodied and restrained on the floor outside the cockpit -- told him he was from Oman. Musaev said that at one point the suspect asked Musaev to kill him. "He said, 'Kill me please, kill me please,'" Musaev said. Israeli officials are expected to be on the ground and involved in the questioning of Al Hammami, sources said. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday said that the suspected attacker, who he didn't name, had undergone "Islamist radicalization." A representative for the school in Australia declined to comment and referred an inquiry from ABC News to the Australian federal police. sources.title: a16z’s Aerie Takes Aim at Blockchain’s Post-Quantum Signature Bottleneck - Crypto Economy
passages: a16z crypto researcher Justin Thaler, alongside a team of co-authors, introduced Aerie.
It is a new proving system designed to aggregate large batches of post-quantum digital signatures into a single computational proof.

This breakthrough directly addresses one of the biggest technical challenges currently facing Proof-of-Stake (PoS) blockchain networks as they attempt to shield themselves against the future threat of quantum computers.
1/ Today we’re releasing Aerie: fast post-quantum signature aggregation, using lattice-based SNARKs for lattice-based Falcon signatures.
If thousands of these signatures were included in the blocks without an effective compression or aggregation method, the bandwidth requirements and costs of operating a node would skyrocket.
However, BLS signatures are based on elliptic curve cryptography, which is theoretically vulnerable to a sufficiently powerful quantum computer.

The development of Aerie makes it clear that designing quantum-safe blockchains will require a delicate balance between long-term security, processing speeds, and the operational costs of decentralized infrastructure.

The Falcon verification process demands fewer calculations of this type, allowing the Aerie verifier to check the algebraic requirements more directly, using a short “salt” appended to each signature.

Compared to previous systems, the authors claim that Aerie is about 29 times faster than approaches like Ethereum’s leanVM in certain consensus scenarios, and 1.5 times faster in proving times than Orthus, a prior Falcon signature aggregator.

Furthermore, unlike recursive systems, Aerie proofs currently cannot be merged with each other, which limits their utility in networks where signature collection is distributed across multiple machines asynchronously.
Venture capital division a16z Crypto unveiled Lattice Jolt this Wednesday, a revamped version of its open-source zero-knowledge virtual machine (zkVM).

It is a new proving system designed to aggregate large batches of post-quantum digital signatures into a single computational proof. This breakthrough directly addresses one of the biggest technical challenges currently facing Proof-of-Stake (PoS) blockchain networks as they attempt to shield themselves against the future threat of quantum computers.

— Justin Thaler (@SuccinctJT) October 16, 2026

Proof-of-Stake blockchains, such as Ethereum , rely on validators’ digital signatures to confirm their participation in the network. Currently, Ethereum groups these signatures (known as BLS) into a single consolidated signature per slot, drastically reducing the data load. However, BLS signatures are based on elliptic curve cryptography, which is theoretically vulnerable to a sufficiently powerful quantum computer.

To solve this, the industry is turning its attention to post-quantum signature schemes (such as Falcon). The problem lies in the fact that the size of these signatures is much larger. A Falcon-512 signature occupies about 666 bytes, compared to the 64 bytes of current signatures. If thousands of these signatures were included in the blocks without an effective compression or aggregation method, the bandwidth requirements and costs of operating a node would skyrocket.

Aerie combines Falcon signatures with a mathematical proving system that is lattice-based. Thaler explained through an X thread that this contrasts with other current approaches, such as Ethereum’s leanVM , which use purely hash-based systems.

Hash-based signatures require the calculation of hundreds of these mathematical functions to be verified, which is highly costly to process in a zero-knowledge proof (ZK-proof) system. The Falcon verification process demands fewer calculations of this type, allowing the Aerie verifier to check the algebraic requirements more directly, using a short “salt” appended to each signature.
According to the published research paper (whose code is already hosted on GitHub with the collaboration of LayerZero Labs), Aerie’s performance is remarkable. In the performance benchmarks:

Compared to previous systems, the authors claim that Aerie is about 29 times faster than approaches like Ethereum’s leanVM in certain consensus scenarios, and 1.5 times faster in proving times than Orthus, a prior Falcon signature aggregator.

However, despite its speed, Aerie presents certain design trade-offs. The proving system (prover) must hold all the signatures of a batch in memory simultaneously, reaching a peak of 2.1 GiB for a batch of 32,768 signatures. Furthermore, unlike recursive systems, Aerie proofs currently cannot be merged with each other, which limits their utility in networks where signature collection is distributed across multiple machines asynchronously.

The development of Aerie makes it clear that designing quantum-safe blockchains will require a delicate balance between long-term security, processing speeds, and the operational costs of decentralized infrastructure.

The proposal uses a mechanism called a degriefer to distinguish legitimate transactions from conflicting spends.
Its stated goal is to reduce on-chain data storage, with a proposed transaction size of 96 bytes.
a16z crypto researcher Justin Thaler and co-authors have introduced Aerie, a proof system designed to aggregate large batches of post-quantum digital signatures into a single proof.

The research addresses a challenge for proof-of-stake blockchains exploring quantum-resistant cryptography : post-quantum signatures are generally larger than current signatures and cannot be aggregated using the same method as Ethereum ’s BLS signatures.
The paper identifies Falcon as one option for post-quantum blockchain applications.
Thaler argued that lattice-based cryptography should remain under consideration as blockchains develop post-quantum systems.
He said lattice-based proofs could reduce reliance on recursive proofs and custom hash-based signatures.
BLS signatures rely on elliptic-curve cryptography, which is considered vulnerable to sufficiently powerful quantum computers.
The paper reports that Aerie’s Falcon-512 aggregate measured approximately 42.1 bytes per signature, making it around 16 times smaller than the original signatures.
The authors also said Aerie exceeded the 1,000-signatures-per-second target cited for Ethereum’s lean consensus effort.
It also discloses that Thaler is an investor in blockchain-based platforms through a16z.
Further evaluation will be needed to assess Aerie’s suitability for distributed blockchain consensus.
These constraints mean that proving speed alone does not establish whether Aerie is suitable for replacing existing aggregation systems in blockchain consensus.
Changes to the final standard could affect aspects of Aerie’s design, including message hashing.
Aerie combines Falcon signatures with a lattice-based proof system.

extraction.body: Aerie aggregates 32,768 Falcon-512 signatures in 0.65 seconds on an Apple M4 Max, with the authors reporting smaller proofs and faster verification. a16z crypto researcher Justin Thaler and co-authors have introduced Aerie, a proof system designed to aggregate large batches of post-quantum digital signatures into a single proof. In an October 16 thread on X, Thaler said Aerie aggregated 32,768 Falcon-512 signatures in 0.65 seconds on an Apple M4 Max laptop CPU. The research addresses a challenge for proof-of-stake blockchains exploring quantum-resistant cryptography : post-quantum signatures are generally larger than current signatures and cannot be aggregated using the same method as Ethereum ’s BLS signatures. 1/ Today we’re releasing Aerie: fast post-quantum signature aggregation , using lattice-based SNARKs for lattice-based Falcon signatures. On a laptop (CPU only), it aggregates roughly a full Ethereum slot’s worth of signatures (32,768) in 0.65 seconds. The team published a research paper hosted by LayerZero Labs and released the implementation code on GitHub. Proof-of-stake blockchains use digital signatures to verify validator participation. Ethereum aggregates validator BLS signatures into a single signature for each slot, reducing the data required to verify participation. BLS signatures rely on elliptic-curve cryptography, which is considered vulnerable to sufficiently powerful quantum computers. Post-quantum signature schemes are designed to resist such attacks, but their larger signatures can increase bandwidth requirements and verification costs. The paper identifies Falcon as one option for post-quantum blockchain applications. A Falcon-512 signature occupies 666 bytes, compared with approximately 64 bytes for the elliptic-curve signatures commonly used today. Without an effective aggregation method, including large numbers of post-quantum signatures in blockchain blocks could increase data requirements and the costs of operating a node . Aerie combines Falcon signatures with a lattice-based proof system. This differs from approaches that use hash-based signatures and hash-based proofs, including the approach associated with Ethereum’s leanVM. According to Thaler’s X thread , Aerie uses Akita, a lattice-based commitment scheme developed with LayerZero Labs, alongside sum-check proving techniques associated with Lattice Jolt. Thaler said hash-based signatures can require hundreds of hash calculations to verify, making them expensive to prove within a zero-knowledge proof system. Falcon’s verification process involves less hashing, allowing Aerie’s verifier to calculate message hashes directly using a short salt attached to each signature. According to the authors, this allows Aerie to prove the remaining algebraic checks without proving the hash computations. Unlike some alternative systems, Aerie does not use recursive proof merging. The paper reports that Aerie’s Falcon-512 aggregate measured approximately 42.1 bytes per signature, making it around 16 times smaller than the original signatures. For Falcon-1024, a stronger parameter variant, the authors report aggregating 16,384 signatures in 0.63 seconds, with a 29-fold reduction in size. The researchers also compared Aerie with Ethereum’s leanVM approach and Orthus, a previous Falcon signature aggregator . Their reported results include: The authors said Orthus does not prove every requirement of the Falcon specification, including its byte-format rules. This qualification matters when interpreting the comparison. The authors also said Aerie exceeded the 1,000-signatures-per-second target cited for Ethereum’s lean consensus effort. Most major blockchains besides Bitcoin run on proof of stake, where validators vote on each block by signing it. Signature aggregation is what makes large validator sets practical. Ethereum uses BLS signatures, whose algebraic structure lets it combine tens of thousands of validator signatures every slot into a single group element. Solana, where validator votes have made up about three-quarters of all transactions, is adopting BLS aggregation too, as part of its Alpenglow upgrade. But as useful as BLS is, it is not post-quantum — and in fact, no known post-quantum signature scheme aggregates this way. Post-quantum signatures are also 10 to 100 times larger than today’s elliptic-curve signatures, so without aggregation these signatures will bloat blocks — limiting throughput and raising the cost of running a node. This matters as blockchains carry a growing share of the world’s payments, from stablecoin transfers to payments made by AI agents. SNARKs (Succinct Non-interactive Arguments of Knowledge) fix these issues: The “aggregate signature” becomes a single succinct proof that every signature in the batch verifies. The prevailing SNARK-based approach, central to Ethereum’s roadmap, pairs hash-based signatures with hash-based SNARKs. But this approach is slow because hash-based signatures are expensive to prove: A single laptop can’t keep up with a full slot of signatures, which is one reason Ethereum’s design splits the work across many provers and recursively merges their proofs. That’s why today we’re releasing Aerie , which takes the opposite approach by aggregating lattice-based signatures using lattice-based SNARKs . Aerie supports Falcon, a lattice-based signature scheme that NIST has selected for standardization, in both its Falcon-512 and Falcon-1024 variants. Aerie is fast enough that a single laptop can aggregate roughly an Ethereum slot’s worth of signatures on its own: Aerie’s speed also makes a simpler aggregation design possible. In Ethereum’s current plan, each proof from leanVM (the zkVM being developed as part of Lean Ethereum to aggregate hash-based signatures) covers only about 900 signatures. Covering a full slot therefore takes rounds of recursive merging, and each round can’t start until the previous round’s proofs arrive. The first is Akita (the lattice-based polynomial commitment scheme we built with LayerZero Labs ), together with the sum-check-based proving techniques we developed on the road to Lattice Jolt. These techniques are highly parallel and well suited to GPUs , so Aerie has plenty of room to get even faster. The second reason Aerie is fast is the relative lack of hashing in lattice signature verification. Hash-based signatures are verified by evaluating hundreds of hashes per signature. Aggregating them means proving all of those hash evaluations — and hashing is expensive to prove, typically adding over 100x overhead relative to computing the hash natively. Lattice signatures are verified differently. The core checks are algebraic, and hashing plays only a small role: a handful of hash evaluations per signature, not hundreds. Falcon takes the lack of hashing especially far. It’s a hash-and-sign scheme whose hash takes only the message and a salt as input. So if the aggregate includes each signature’s salt, the verifier can compute every hash itself, and the proof needs to cover only the algebraic checks. That’s a big part of Aerie’s speed, and why we started with Falcon. Falcon is also compact: Falcon-1024 reaches NIST’s highest security level with signatures about half the size of ML-DSA-44’s, the lowest-security ML-DSA parameter set. We’re not suggesting every blockchain adopt Falcon. Its signing algorithm is complex, and it has historically been hard to fit on hardware wallets, relying on floating-point arithmetic and tens of kilobytes of working memory. Side-channel hardening is still an active area of work. But these drawbacks are being addressed rapidly. Recent research has shown how to implement Falcon signing with fixed-point arithmetic instead of floating point, and NIST now plans to require this approach in the FN-DSA standard. A new implementation also cuts Falcon-512 signing to about 11 kB of RAM, small enough for the secure elements in hardware wallets. For both reasons, Falcon is far easier to deploy than it was even a year ago. Hardware wallets are a challenge for stateless hash-based signatures too: The SPHINCS- variants light enough for a hardware wallet take from 47 seconds to over six minutes to sign on a Ledger secure element. For chains that weigh Falcon’s trade-offs and choose it — as Solana is exploring and Algorand has deployed — Aerie offers a fast path to aggregation. We’re also working on extensions that require proving some hashing: supporting ML-DSA, whose hash depends on the signature itself; and removing Falcon’s salts from the aggregate by proving its hash inside the SNARK. Recent advances like LaBinius offer paths to proving those few hashes efficiently. And we’re extending Aerie to hybrid signatures that pair a lattice signature with an elliptic-curve-based one, an important form of defense-in-depth. These extensions may not reach 50,000 signatures per second, but we still expect plenty of headroom over the 1,000 per second Ethereum has targeted . There’s an active debate about lattice versus hash-based cryptography in blockchain design, sharpened by speculation about what AI might mean for cryptanalysis . We’ll make the full case for embracing lattices in a future post. The short version is this: No one can promise that new attacks won’t be found on lattices, or on any other cryptography. But speculative cryptanalytic risk must be weighed against the clear and present risks built into more complicated systems. As noted above, Ethereum’s planned hash-only signature aggregation design relies on SNARK recursion, with the coordination overhead, bug surface, and unestablished security that come with that approach. Hash-only designs also lean on non-standard constructions: Ethereum’s planned consensus and account signatures are custom schemes outside NIST’s standards, with the underlying hash still undecided. This limits support from hardware wallets for individual users, and from the hardware security modules and custody systems that institutions rely on. Private payments need encryption, not just signatures and proofs: Recipients must learn about the notes sent to them, viewing keys must grant read access, and encrypted mempools must hide transactions until they’re ordered. Private payments matter to cypherpunks and financial institutions alike, and Ethereum already plans for them. The Ethereum Foundation’s strawmap , a draft long-term roadmap for its base layer, lists a private L1 with shielded transfers among its five “north stars,” alongside a hash-based post-quantum L1. Those two goals are in tension: Shielded transfers need encryption, and encryption is exactly what hashing alone cannot provide. Those two goals are in tension: Shielded transfers need encryption, yet encryption is exactly what hashing alone cannot provide. A classic result of Russell Impagliazzo and Steven Rudich shows that public-key encryption cannot be built from hash functions in a black-box way. The best hash-only alternative, Merkle puzzles , gives honest users only a quadratic advantage over attackers, and this is optimal : No protocol can do better when hashes are modeled as random oracles. Even advocates of hash-only designs acknowledge this. So a private Ethereum, like any chain that supports private payments, will depend on structured cryptography somewhere in its stack — and in practice, that means lattices. ML-KEM, a lattice scheme, is NIST’s primary post-quantum encryption standard and is already deployed across much of the internet . Are there workarounds? One proposed solution is to keep encrypted notes off-chain, so fewer ciphertexts sit in public forever. But this doesn’t avoid encryption: The notes must still reach their recipients encrypted, over messaging apps and other channels that are already moving to ML-KEM. And off-chain delivery has trade-offs of its own: a channel that must stay available, can observe metadata, and whose failure can leave recipients unable to find and spend their funds. For post-quantum blockchains with privacy, then, avoiding lattices in signatures and proofs doesn’t actually remove the dependence on lattices; it just gives up the performance and simplicity lattices offer — the costs, without the benefits. So the real question isn’t whether to rely on lattices, but whether to forgo their benefits for a false sense of security. An Aerie proof is about 66 KiB, whether it covers 32,768 Falcon-512 signatures or 16,384 Falcon-1024 signatures. That’s on par with the most compact prior lattice-based approach: PSE’s benchmarks of LaBRADOR-based Falcon aggregation report about 74 KB for 10,000 signatures, though verification there takes seconds rather than milliseconds. Because Aerie’s verifier computes each signature’s hash itself, it also needs each signature’s 40-byte salt. For large batches, the salts dominate: 32,768 of them take up about 1.3 MB, versus 66 KiB for the proof. Even so, the aggregate costs only about 42 bytes per signature, 16 times smaller than Falcon-512 signatures (666 bytes) and nearly 30 times smaller than Falcon-1024 signatures (1,280 bytes). Some deployments avoid the salt cost entirely. Algorand’s deterministic Falcon makes signing deterministic, which lets it replace the random per-signature salt with a fixed value. Aggregating its signatures would need no salts at all, just the 66 KiB proof, with small changes to how Aerie handles the salt and signature encoding. Measured against Falcon itself, Aerie’s prover is also cheap : On a single core, proving takes only about 8 times as long as standard Falcon verification of the same signatures, and 1.4 times as long as signing them. Compared with Orthus , the fastest prior Falcon aggregation scheme, Aerie (on one core of the same AVX-512 server): Moreover, Aerie proves everything a standard Falcon verifier checks. Prior Falcon aggregation work did not: It left out the check that each signature is canonically encoded, so its aggregates could accept signatures that a standard Falcon verifier would reject. We also compared Aerie with leanVM , which aggregates XMSS signatures, the stateful hash-based scheme Ethereum plans to use for consensus. On the same machine, Aerie aggregates 29x as many signatures per second (about 50,800 versus 1,770). Stateful signatures like XMSS work well at the consensus layer, where each validator signs at most one message per slot, so the slot number itself can serve as the signing state. But they pose large risks at the execution layer: A user who signs from two devices, or restores a wallet from a backup, can reuse signing state and thereby let attackers forge signatures under their key. That’s why Ethereum plans a stateless hash-based scheme for account signatures. And stateless hash-based signatures are even costlier to aggregate: In leanVM’s latest published benchmarks , on the same laptop model, it aggregates them at about 820 per second, roughly 60x slower than Aerie. (The benchmarked configuration also caps each key at about 127,000 signatures; configurations that allow far more cost more at key generation but aggregate just as fast.)
