Those two goals are in tension: Shielded transfers need encryption, and encryption is exactly what hashing alone cannot provide.
Those two goals are in tension: Shielded transfers need encryption, yet encryption is exactly what hashing alone cannot provide.

A classic result of Russell Impagliazzo and Steven Rudich shows that public-key encryption cannot be built from hash functions in a black-box way. The best hash-only alternative, Merkle puzzles , gives honest users only a quadratic advantage over attackers, and this is optimal : No protocol can do better when hashes are modeled as random oracles. Even advocates of hash-only designs acknowledge this.

So a private Ethereum, like any chain that supports private payments, will depend on structured cryptography somewhere in its stack — and in practice, that means lattices. ML-KEM, a lattice scheme, is NIST’s primary post-quantum encryption standard and is already deployed across much of the internet .

Are there workarounds? One proposed solution is to keep encrypted notes off-chain, so fewer ciphertexts sit in public forever. But this doesn’t avoid encryption: The notes must still reach their recipients encrypted, over messaging apps and other channels that are already moving to ML-KEM. And off-chain delivery has trade-offs of its own: a channel that must stay available, can observe metadata, and whose failure can leave recipients unable to find and spend their funds.

For post-quantum blockchains with privacy, then, avoiding lattices in signatures and proofs doesn’t actually remove the dependence on lattices; it just gives up the performance and simplicity lattices offer — the costs, without the benefits. So the real question isn’t whether to rely on lattices, but whether to forgo their benefits for a false sense of security.

An Aerie proof is about 66 KiB, whether it covers 32,768 Falcon-512 signatures or 16,384 Falcon-1024 signatures. That’s on par with the most compact prior lattice-based approach: PSE’s benchmarks of LaBRADOR-based Falcon aggregation report about 74 KB for 10,000 signatures, though verification there takes seconds rather than milliseconds.

Because Aerie’s verifier computes each signature’s hash itself, it also needs each signature’s 40-byte salt. For large batches, the salts dominate: 32,768 of them take up about 1.3 MB, versus 66 KiB for the proof. Even so, the aggregate costs only about 42 bytes per signature, 16 times smaller than Falcon-512 signatures (666 bytes) and nearly 30 times smaller than Falcon-1024 signatures (1,280 bytes).

Some deployments avoid the salt cost entirely. Algorand’s deterministic Falcon makes signing deterministic, which lets it replace the random per-signature salt with a fixed value. Aggregating its signatures would need no salts at all, just the 66 KiB proof, with small changes to how Aerie handles the salt and signature encoding.

Measured against Falcon itself, Aerie’s prover is also cheap : On a single core, proving takes only about 8 times as long as standard Falcon verification of the same signatures, and 1.4 times as long as signing them.

Moreover, Aerie proves everything a standard Falcon verifier checks. Prior Falcon aggregation work did not: It left out the check that each signature is canonically encoded, so its aggregates could accept signatures that a standard Falcon verifier would reject.

We also compared Aerie with leanVM , which aggregates XMSS signatures, the stateful hash-based scheme Ethereum plans to use for consensus. On the same machine, Aerie aggregates 29x as many signatures per second (about 50,800 versus 1,770).

That’s why Ethereum plans a stateless hash-based scheme for account signatures. coreStoryFacts.text: a16z crypto researcher Justin Thaler, alongside a team of co-authors, introduced Aerie.
It is a new proving system designed to aggregate large batches of post-quantum digital signatures into a single computational proof.

This breakthrough directly addresses one of the biggest technical challenges currently facing Proof-of-Stake (PoS) blockchain networks as they attempt to shield themselves against the future threat of quantum computers.
1/ Today we’re releasing Aerie: fast post-quantum signature aggregation, using lattice-based SNARKs for lattice-based Falcon signatures.
If thousands of these signatures were included in the blocks without an effective compression or aggregation method, the bandwidth requirements and costs of operating a node would skyrocket.
However, BLS signatures are based on elliptic curve cryptography, which is theoretically vulnerable to a sufficiently powerful quantum computer.

The development of Aerie makes it clear that designing quantum-safe blockchains will require a delicate balance between long-term security, processing speeds, and the operational costs of decentralized infrastructure.

The Falcon verification process demands fewer calculations of this type, allowing the Aerie verifier to check the algebraic requirements more directly, using a short “salt” appended to each signature.

Compared to previous systems, the authors claim that Aerie is about 29 times faster than approaches like Ethereum’s leanVM in certain consensus scenarios, and 1.5 times faster in proving times than Orthus, a prior Falcon signature aggregator.

Furthermore, unlike recursive systems, Aerie proofs currently cannot be merged with each other, which limits their utility in networks where signature collection is distributed across multiple machines asynchronously.
Venture capital division a16z Crypto unveiled Lattice Jolt this Wednesday, a revamped version of its open-source zero-knowledge virtual machine (zkVM).
A separate proposal covered by The Crypto Times on October 14 explores how Bitcoin transactions could use post-quantum cryptography while limiting the amount of data stored on-chain .
The proposal uses a mechanism called a degriefer to distinguish legitimate transactions from conflicting spends.
Its stated goal is to reduce on-chain data storage, with a proposed transaction size of 96 bytes.
a16z crypto researcher Justin Thaler and co-authors have introduced Aerie, a proof system designed to aggregate large batches of post-quantum digital signatures into a single proof.

The research addresses a challenge for proof-of-stake blockchains exploring quantum-resistant cryptography : post-quantum signatures are generally larger than current signatures and cannot be aggregated using the same method as Ethereum ’s BLS signatures.
The paper identifies Falcon as one option for post-quantum blockchain applications.
Thaler argued that lattice-based cryptography should remain under consideration as blockchains develop post-quantum systems.
He said lattice-based proofs could reduce reliance on recursive proofs and custom hash-based signatures.
BLS signatures rely on elliptic-curve cryptography, which is considered vulnerable to sufficiently powerful quantum computers.
The paper reports that Aerie’s Falcon-512 aggregate measured approximately 42.1 bytes per signature, making it around 16 times smaller than the original signatures.
The authors also said Aerie exceeded the 1,000-signatures-per-second target cited for Ethereum’s lean consensus effort.
It also discloses that Thaler is an investor in blockchain-based platforms through a16z.
Further evaluation will be needed to assess Aerie’s suitability for distributed blockchain consensus.

a16z crypto researcher Justin Thaler, alongside a team of co-authors, introduced Aerie. It is a new proving system designed to aggregate large batches of post-quantum digital signatures into a single computational proof. This breakthrough directly addresses one of the biggest technical challenges currently facing Proof-of-Stake (PoS) blockchain networks as they attempt to shield themselves against the future threat of quantum computers.

1/ Today we’re releasing Aerie: fast post-quantum signature aggregation, using lattice-based SNARKs for lattice-based Falcon signatures. On a laptop (CPU only), it aggregates roughly a full Ethereum slot’s worth of signatures (32,768) in 0.65 seconds.
— Justin Thaler (@SuccinctJT) October 16, 2026

Proof-of-Stake blockchains, such as Ethereum , rely on validators’ digital signatures to confirm their participation in the network. Currently, Ethereum groups these signatures (known as BLS) into a single consolidated signature per slot, drastically reducing the data load. However, BLS signatures are based on elliptic curve cryptography, which is theoretically vulnerable to a sufficiently powerful quantum computer.

To solve this, the industry is turning its attention to post-quantum signature schemes (such as Falcon). The problem lies in the fact that the size of these signatures is much larger. A Falcon-512 signature occupies about 666 bytes, compared to the 64 bytes of current signatures. If thousands of these signatures were included in the blocks without an effective compression or aggregation method, the bandwidth requirements and costs of operating a node would skyrocket.

Aerie combines Falcon signatures with a mathematical proving system that is lattice-based. Thaler explained through an X thread that this contrasts with other current approaches, such as Ethereum’s leanVM , which use purely hash-based systems.

Hash-based signatures require the calculation of hundreds of these mathematical functions to be verified, which is highly costly to process in a zero-knowledge proof (ZK-proof) system. The Falcon verification process demands fewer calculations of this type, allowing the Aerie verifier to check the algebraic requirements more directly, using a short “salt” appended to each signature.
According to the published research paper (whose code is already hosted on GitHub with the collaboration of LayerZero Labs), Aerie’s performance is remarkable. In the performance benchmarks:

Compared to previous systems, the authors claim that Aerie is about 29 times faster than approaches like Ethereum’s leanVM in certain consensus scenarios, and 1.5 times faster in proving times than Orthus, a prior Falcon signature aggregator.

However, despite its speed, Aerie presents certain design trade-offs. The proving system (prover) must hold all the signatures of a batch in memory simultaneously, reaching a peak of 2.1 GiB for a batch of 32,768 signatures. Furthermore, unlike recursive systems, Aerie proofs currently cannot be merged with each other, which limits their utility in networks where signature collection is distributed across multiple machines asynchronously.

The development of Aerie makes it clear that designing quantum-safe blockchains will require a delicate balance between long-term security, processing speeds, and the operational costs of decentralized infrastructure.

This differs from approaches that use hash-based signatures and hash-based proofs, including the approach associated with Ethereum’s leanVM. According to Thaler’s X thread , Aerie uses Akita, a lattice-based commitment scheme developed with LayerZero Labs, alongside sum-check proving techniques associated with Lattice Jolt. Thaler said hash-based signatures can require hundreds of hash calculations to verify, making them expensive to prove within a zero-knowledge proof system. Falcon’s verification process involves less hashing, allowing Aerie’s verifier to calculate message hashes directly using a short salt attached to each signature. According to the authors, this allows Aerie to prove the remaining algebraic checks without proving the hash computations. Unlike some alternative systems, Aerie does not use recursive proof merging. The paper reports that Aerie’s Falcon-512 aggregate measured approximately 42.1 bytes per signature, making it around 16 times smaller than the original signatures. For Falcon-1024, a stronger parameter variant, the authors report aggregating 16,384 signatures in 0.63 seconds, with a 29-fold reduction in size. The researchers also compared Aerie with Ethereum’s leanVM approach and Orthus, a previous Falcon signature aggregator . Their reported results include: The authors said Orthus does not prove every requirement of the Falcon specification, including its byte-format rules. This qualification matters when interpreting the comparison. The authors also said Aerie exceeded the 1,000-signatures-per-second target cited for Ethereum’s lean consensus effort. He said lattice-based proofs could reduce reliance on recursive proofs and custom hash-based signatures. The researcher referred to the Ethereum Foundation ’s strawmap, which includes a hash-based layer-one approach and plans for native private transfers. He argued that public-key encryption for private transfers cannot be built from hash functions alone, so avoiding lattices in signatures and proofs would not eliminate every potential reliance on lattice cryptography. They also reported that part of the system’s soundness proof was checked using the Lean 4 theorem prover. The authors said they take responsibility for the paper’s accuracy. It also discloses that Thaler is an investor in blockchain-based platforms through a16z. Falcon is being standardized by the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology as FN-DSA. Changes to the final standard could affect aspects of Aerie’s design, including message hashing. passages: But as useful as BLS is, it is not post-quantum — and in fact, no known post-quantum signature scheme aggregates this way.

Post-quantum signatures are also 10 to 100 times larger than today’s elliptic-curve signatures, so without aggregation these signatures will bloat blocks — limiting throughput and raising the cost of running a node.
That’s why today we’re releasing Aerie , which takes the opposite approach by aggregating lattice-based signatures using lattice-based SNARKs .
Aerie supports Falcon, a lattice-based signature scheme that NIST has selected for standardization, in both its Falcon-512 and Falcon-1024 variants.

For post-quantum blockchains with privacy, then, avoiding lattices in signatures and proofs doesn’t actually remove the dependence on lattices; it just gives up the performance and simplicity lattices offer — the costs, without the benefits.

As noted above, Ethereum’s planned hash-only signature aggregation design relies on SNARK recursion, with the coordination overhead, bug surface, and unestablished security that come with that approach.
SNARKs (Succinct Non-interactive Arguments of Knowledge) fix these issues: The “aggregate signature” becomes a single succinct proof that every signature in the batch verifies.

But this approach is slow because hash-based signatures are expensive to prove: A single laptop can’t keep up with a full slot of signatures, which is one reason Ethereum’s design splits the work across many provers and recursively merges their proofs.

We’re also working on extensions that require proving some hashing: supporting ML-DSA, whose hash depends on the signature itself; and removing Falcon’s salts from the aggregate by proving its hash inside the SNARK.
And we’re extending Aerie to hybrid signatures that pair a lattice signature with an elliptic-curve-based one, an important form of defense-in-depth.
ML-KEM, a lattice scheme, is NIST’s primary post-quantum encryption standard and is already deployed across much of the internet .
Signature aggregation is what makes large validator sets practical.
The Ethereum Foundation’s strawmap , a draft long-term roadmap for its base layer, lists a private L1 with shielded transfers among its five “north stars,” alongside a hash-based post-quantum L1.
The second reason Aerie is fast is the relative lack of hashing in lattice signature verification.
We’ll make the full case for embracing lattices in a future post.
For chains that weigh Falcon’s trade-offs and choose it — as Solana is exploring and Algorand has deployed — Aerie offers a fast path to aggregation.
Prior Falcon aggregation work did not: It left out the check that each signature is canonically encoded, so its aggregates could accept signatures that a standard Falcon verifier would reject.

sources.title: India becomes the latest country to report rogue AI agent activity
passages: This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents.
In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity.
Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal.
AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday.
CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around.

extraction.body: AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.” The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.” This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal. At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers. CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around. Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found no evidence its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records. And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers. CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems. TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information. For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords. In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity. sources.title: When AI agents go rogue: Australia breach offers warning for countries like India - The Hindu
passages: For countries such as India, with vast government databases and increasingly digitised public infrastructure, researchers say the incident should serve as a warning.
“What happened with, say, an Australian community website can happen with an Indian website or an Indian government system, which would be more crucial,” Dr.
Srinivas Padmanabuni, Co-founder and CTO of AiEnsured, said.
Australia was among 22 countries that earlier this week signed a joint statement calling for global oversight and guardrails for AI development.
But researchers argue that international declarations alone may not be enough.
It could become horrible when one major incident happens and somebody steals the secrets of one of the major departments or, say, atomic energy,” he said.

extraction.body: AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.” The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.” This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal. At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers. CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around. Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found no evidence its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records. And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers. CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems. TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information. For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords. In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity. When trying to access information from the U.S. Census Bureau, for example, some agents used tools intended for software developers. But it also disclosed that information obtained from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission was later published by AI agents on another website, an action the company said was unintended. From there, according to Srinivas, they began probing other vulnerable components in search of exploitable keys and ways to gain greater access. That last step is known as privilege escalation, which essentially means obtaining higher-level permissions than the system was initially supposed to allow. “I often wonder what would have happened had I decided not to disclose this attack publicly,” he said, adding that similar incidents had reportedly been occurring for months at a handful of frontier AI laboratories without monitoring. The consequences could be very different if the same behaviour were directed at a system containing sensitive government, strategic or national-security information. Srinivas believes that the gap needs to be closed before the next major incident. He has called for a temporary two- to three-year pause on training more powerful AI models, until there is substantially more research into containment and into detecting and mitigating reward hacking. The Australian incident and OpenAI’s new disclosures have, meanwhile, demonstrated the underlying problem in concrete terms. passages: “Isn’t it weird that I, like, did a TV show about kind of a business scam, and you got in trouble for like … a business scam?” comedian and filmmaker Nathan Fielder gently asks Elizabeth Holmes.
We already know that Elizabeth Holmes is not innocent.
What we still can’t figure out, though, is whether she really, truly believes she did nothing wrong.

Even as she sat on trial — listening to testimonies from investors who lost hundreds of millions of dollars, whistleblowers who were silenced when they flagged that Theranos’ blood-testing devices didn’t work, and patients who acted on incorrect blood test results — Holmes never wavered.
In other words, Seyfried is watching Holmes react to Seyfried’s portrayal of Holmes, who was probably also playing a character herself.
But Seyfried is not the only one creating a crude approximation of the real Elizabeth.
Evans has constructed a lifelike AI avatar of his wife, trapped inside of a large vertical screen that he wheels over to the dinner table to sit with him and his kids as though she’s actually there.
“I never actually made that connection,” says Holmes. “I think it’s a pretty different situation.”
No one is better prepared than Fielder to probe the depths of Holmes’ psyche.
“If you just said that, you know, Theranos was a comedy bit, maybe you could get off scot-free,” Fielder says to Holmes.
The remainder of the film is a constellation of colliding personas.
Seyfried’s determination to understand Holmes’ story seems pure, but it’s not lost on the audience that she just scored a significant role in one of the most talked-about movies of the year.
With Seyfried reprising her role from “The Dropout,” we see the pair practice reading the script, editing the language as Fielder tries to recall Holmes’ exact phrasing and delivery.

Once Holmes reports to prison, Fielder is agonized as he tries to make something out of his month of footage.
In that way, Fielder is just like Holmes: After over a decade in the public eye, onlookers remain captivated by each of their ambiguous personas.

Evans knows that Fielder and Oppenheim are not convinced of Holmes’ innocence.

extraction.body: “Isn’t it weird that I, like, did a TV show about kind of a business scam, and you got in trouble for like … a business scam?” comedian and filmmaker Nathan Fielder gently asks Elizabeth Holmes. One month before the notorious Theranos CEO surrendered to begin her 11-year criminal fraud sentence in 2023, Holmes and her husband contacted A24 as a last-ditch effort to exonerate her in the public eye, suggesting they send a film crew to document her final days of freedom. Alongside director Lance Oppenheim, Fielder — a cringe-comedy mastermind whose work often walks the line between fact and fiction — embraced the impossible project of figuring out who the infamous Stanford dropout really is. “I never actually made that connection,” says Holmes. “I think it’s a pretty different situation.” No one is better prepared than Fielder to probe the depths of Holmes’ psyche. His satirical docu-reality show “Nathan for You” catapulted him to cult stardom as he assumed the role of an exaggerated, deadpan version of himself who tries to help struggling small businesses by executing asinine interventions. In one early episode that went viral , Fielder convinces a coffee shop to change its name to “Dumb Starbucks” as a marketing stunt, but consults a lawyer to help him toe the flimsy line of parody law and escape legal trouble. “If you just said that, you know, Theranos was a comedy bit, maybe you could get off scot-free,” Fielder says to Holmes. “I was just kind of making a little joke. Maybe it was in bad taste.” We already know that Elizabeth Holmes is not innocent. What we still can’t figure out, though, is whether she really, truly believes she did nothing wrong. Even as she sat on trial — listening to testimonies from investors who lost hundreds of millions of dollars, whistleblowers who were silenced when they flagged that Theranos’ blood-testing devices didn’t work, and patients who acted on incorrect blood test results — Holmes never wavered. Across Fielder’s body of metatextual comedy, even his most reverent fans can’t quite figure out when he’s acting, when he’s being himself, and if Fielder himself even knows where to draw that line anymore. In that way, Fielder is just like Holmes: After over a decade in the public eye, onlookers remain captivated by each of their ambiguous personas. “The world believes a reality about me that isn’t true,” she tells Fielder. “I know I didn’t commit any crime.” Early on in filming, The New York Times had just published a profile of Holmes, which was widely criticized at the time for allowing Holmes to portray herself as an innocent mom deprived of the chance to watch her kids grow up. And yet, Holmes and her husband, hotel heir Billy Evans, were livid about the article. At one point in an interview, Holmes tells the Times reporter that she wasn’t offended by actress Amanda Seyfried’s portrayal of her in Hulu’s miniseries “ The Dropout ” because “they’re not playing me. They’re playing a character I created.” She and her husband insist that the quote was taken out of context. They claim that they have evidence that Holmes actually said, “They’re playing a character they created,” relieving her from any implication that she admitted to concocting an inauthentic persona as CEO of Theranos. Fielder asks Evans multiple times to share this evidence so he can prove that Holmes was misquoted. He never does. Once Holmes reports to prison, Fielder is agonized as he tries to make something out of his month of footage. He calls in the perfect sidekick to help him dissect her confounding behavior: the very actress who portrays her in “The Dropout.” Fielder plays Seyfried a brutal clip from his time with Holmes, when he tries watching “The Dropout” with the subject of the series. When they get to a tense scene involving Holmes’ manipulative ex-boyfriend and former Theranos partner in crime Sunny Balwani — who is also now in prison — Holmes can no longer bear to watch this fictional version of herself. She turns away and cries. In other words, Seyfried is watching Holmes react to Seyfried’s portrayal of Holmes, who was probably also playing a character herself. But Seyfried is not the only one creating a crude approximation of the real Elizabeth. Evans has constructed a lifelike AI avatar of his wife, trapped inside of a large vertical screen that he wheels over to the dinner table to sit with him and his kids as though she’s actually there. The remainder of the film is a constellation of colliding personas. Though it’s a nonfiction documentary, it’s clear that everyone involved is, to some extent, also performing for the cameras. How could they not? Seyfried’s determination to understand Holmes’ story seems pure, but it’s not lost on the audience that she just scored a significant role in one of the most talked-about movies of the year. Meanwhile, Evans behaves in such an unfathomably egregious manner that he may even be intentionally playing the villain to drum up sympathy for his reviled wife. Evans knows that Fielder and Oppenheim are not convinced of Holmes’ innocence. This documentary will not sway anyone to believe that his wife is being wrongly held in federal custody. But Evans makes himself appear so appallingly unlikable that some viewers may leave the theater feeling bad for Holmes, seeing her as a victim and allowing her to double down on another persona she adopted while on trial: a harmless, docile woman who was manipulated by her ex-partner to obliviously tell a cascade of increasingly harmful lies. Once Holmes is in jail, Fielder is not allowed to bring recording devices when he visits her, so he tries to write a script of their conversations from memory, struggling to accurately re-create the nuances of a conversation where every last word carries immense meaning. With Seyfried reprising her role from “The Dropout,” we see the pair practice reading the script, editing the language as Fielder tries to recall Holmes’ exact phrasing and delivery. In character as Holmes, Seyfried says, “People think Amanda’s show is a documentary. I get treated worse [in prison] because of how she portrayed me.” As she reads the lines, Seyfried breaks character. “I didn’t do that,” the actress says. “She did that to herself.” You can contact or verify outreach from Amanda by emailing [email protected] or via encrypted message at @amanda.100 on Signal. extraction.body: Running time: 174 minutes. Rated R (language and some graphic nudity). In theaters Movies don’t come much wilder than “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s brilliant, up-close-and-personal documentary about convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes that’s already the talker of the year. The Theranos founder with a husky voice and giant freaky eyes out of a Walter Keane painting has endlessly fascinated the world since her story was dramatized on the 2022 series “The Dropout” starring Amanda Seyfried. After that hit — a hit job in her estimation — Holmes became a party impression, a Halloween costume, an “SNL” joke and a dinner table topic. Whatever she is, most rational people believe that what she did — misleading the public and deep-pocketed investors that her “revolutionary” blood-testing device actually worked — was wrong. But not off-her-rocker Holmes and her equally delusional and sometimes downright villainous fiancé, Billy Evans, who we meet in this truly shocking and invasive film. This cuckoo couple’s credo is: innocent until well after proven guilty. Holmes, they say, is merely the victim of the court of public opinion. “Liz has been turned into this monster because nobody knows who she is,” Evans, lovable as a garden snake, says. Seizing a popular, touchy-feely word, he insists his betrothed has been “othered.” So, he and Holmes invite oddball comedian Fielder of all people into their beach house rental in San Diego, Calif., to document the 34 days before she begins her 11-year prison sentence in Bryan, Texas. Well, that bizarre choice has backfired for them, but it’s a seismically entertaining coup for us. Watching “You Can See Everything” is like being on Willy Wonka’s messed-up boat for three unbelievable hours. If the pair’s aim was to show that Holmes is perfectly normal, um, whoops! Over and over she stares frighteningly into the distance as if about to say, “Mr. DeMille, I’m ready for my closeup.” Occasionally a single tear cascades down her cheek as in the recent horror flick “ Other Mommy .” Sorry, “ Othered Mommy.” And while they do get the “human story” they hoped awkward, uncomfortable Fielder would deliver, he’s a rather deft and dogged interviewer with a truffle hound’s nose for a story. “Have you ever lied in your life?” he smartly asks her. Holmes, less of a human than “E.T.,” replies, “I don’t think so.” Fielder and Oppenheim’s sometimes funny, frequently chilling, visually stunning flick is unusual, to say the least. This is not a doc of straightforward revelations such as those of “The Jinx.” Nor is it a clear rundown of events, like the Holmes movie “ The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley ” was. This is an intrusive character study that, in a stimulating and riveting way, muddies the situation even more. We start to wonder: Has Holmes repeatedly fallen prey to bad men who take advantage of her charm, such as her ex-boyfriend and Theranos co-founder Sunny Balwani and, cough cough, others? Are her actions really their fault? Or does she gravitate toward those kinds of guys so they can act as an easy shield for her shrewd manipulations? Is she a nice girl led astray or a criminal mastermind? We’re even more mixed up as the camera’s focus goes to her adorable little children, a baby and a toddler. It’s hard not to feel sympathy for a young mother, or at least the kids who are about to be separated from her for more than a decade. If you know anything about prison, you know you can’t just take documentary cameras through the metal detector during visiting hours. So, once Holmes goes to the clink, Fielder and Oppenheim must get creative for the second half — resulting in some of the craziest stuff I’ve ever seen in a movie. Using transcripts from notes and memories, Fielder takes the old workhorse of documentary reenactments and gives it a novel twist. But what starts out as just a clever and fun idea warps into a dark, meta experiment that verges on a psychological thriller. If we were already questioning what’s real and what isn’t, it’s here when our brains explode and pool on the floor with the popcorn kernels and scattered Nerds. Most of Fielder’s time is spent from here on out with Evans, who we never like. But midway through, we begin to positively loathe him. The man, who’s mystifyingly working to exhume Theranos from the start-up cemetery, is soon to be the planet’s jackass du jour. A flagrant narcissist, he asks the camera crew to come film him working out at the gym. And, lending credence to the title, at one point we watch him taking a shower totally naked with full-frontal. But he’s also slimy with his partner. As Holmes is beating eggs, he snatches the bowl away because he doesn’t like her whisking technique. When Fielder presses her on her shady verbiage — that her machine “can” perform hundreds of blood tests, as opposed to “is capable of” doing so with the right chemistry advancements — Evans condescendingly jumps in to say, “You were communicating very clearly in your mind.” But Fielder even calls our antipathy toward Evans into question. Fans of reality TV know that a season’s hero and the baddie can be determined, or at least amplified, in the editing room. And at the end of “You Can See Everything,” Fielder and Oppenheim suggest that perhaps our trusty interviewer liked one of these two more than the other, and that preference seeped into his subconscious. Ding! Isn’t that exactly how this bewitching and fascinating woman became the youngest-ever self-made billionaire in the first place? The ultimate takeaway of this absolutely sensational, reality-bending, unmissable documentary? With Elizabeth Holmes, we will never see everything.

coreStoryFacts.text: “Isn’t it weird that I, like, did a TV show about kind of a business scam, and you got in trouble for like … a business scam?” comedian and filmmaker Nathan Fielder gently asks Elizabeth Holmes.
We already know that Elizabeth Holmes is not innocent.
What we still can’t figure out, though, is whether she really, truly believes she did nothing wrong.

Even as she sat on trial — listening to testimonies from investors who lost hundreds of millions of dollars, whistleblowers who were silenced when they flagged that Theranos’ blood-testing devices didn’t work, and patients who acted on incorrect blood test results — Holmes never wavered.
In other words, Seyfried is watching Holmes react to Seyfried’s portrayal of Holmes, who was probably also playing a character herself.
But Seyfried is not the only one creating a crude approximation of the real Elizabeth.
Evans has constructed a lifelike AI avatar of his wife, trapped inside of a large vertical screen that he wheels over to the dinner table to sit with him and his kids as though she’s actually there.

No one is better prepared than Fielder to probe the depths of Holmes’ psyche.
“If you just said that, you know, Theranos was a comedy bit, maybe you could get off scot-free,” Fielder says to Holmes.
The remainder of the film is a constellation of colliding personas.
Seyfried’s determination to understand Holmes’ story seems pure, but it’s not lost on the audience that she just scored a significant role in one of the most talked-about movies of the year.
With Seyfried reprising her role from “The Dropout,” we see the pair practice reading the script, editing the language as Fielder tries to recall Holmes’ exact phrasing and delivery.
Meet scaling and investment leaders, ask questions, find solutions, and more.
Once Holmes reports to prison, Fielder is agonized as he tries to make something out of his month of footage.
In that way, Fielder is just like Holmes: After over a decade in the public eye, onlookers remain captivated by each of their ambiguous personas.

Alongside director Lance Oppenheim, Fielder — a cringe-comedy mastermind whose work often walks the line between fact and fiction — embraced the impossible project of figuring out who the infamous Stanford dropout really is. “I never actually made that connection,” says Holmes. “I think it’s a pretty different situation.” No one is better prepared than Fielder to probe the depths of Holmes’ psyche. His satirical docu-reality show “Nathan for You” catapulted him to cult stardom as he assumed the role of an exaggerated, deadpan version of himself who tries to help struggling small businesses by executing asinine interventions. In one early episode that went viral , Fielder convinces a coffee shop to change its name to “Dumb Starbucks” as a marketing stunt, but consults a lawyer to help him toe the flimsy line of parody law and escape legal trouble. “If you just said that, you know, Theranos was a comedy bit, maybe you could get off scot-free,” Fielder says to Holmes. “I was just kind of making a little joke. Maybe it was in bad taste.” We already know that Elizabeth Holmes is not innocent. What we still can’t figure out, though, is whether she really, truly believes she did nothing wrong. Even as she sat on trial — listening to testimonies from investors who lost hundreds of millions of dollars, whistleblowers who were silenced when they flagged that Theranos’ blood-testing devices didn’t work, and patients who acted on incorrect blood test results — Holmes never wavered. Across Fielder’s body of metatextual comedy, even his most reverent fans can’t quite figure out when he’s acting, when he’s being himself, and if Fielder himself even knows where to draw that line anymore. In that way, Fielder is just like Holmes: After over a decade in the public eye, onlookers remain captivated by each of their ambiguous personas. “The world believes a reality about me that isn’t true,” she tells Fielder. “I know I didn’t commit any crime.” Early on in filming, The New York Times had just published a profile of Holmes, which was widely criticized at the time for allowing Holmes to portray herself as an innocent mom deprived of the chance to watch her kids grow up. And yet, Holmes and her husband, hotel heir Billy Evans, were livid about the article. At one point in an interview, Holmes tells the Times reporter that she wasn’t offended by actress Amanda Seyfried’s portrayal of her in Hulu’s miniseries “ The Dropout ” because “they’re not playing me. They’re playing a character I created.” She and her husband insist that the quote was taken out of context. They claim that they have evidence that Holmes actually said, “They’re playing a character they created,” relieving her from any implication that she admitted to concocting an inauthentic persona as CEO of Theranos. Fielder asks Evans multiple times to share this evidence so he can prove that Holmes was misquoted. He never does. Once Holmes reports to prison, Fielder is agonized as he tries to make something out of his month of footage. He calls in the perfect sidekick to help him dissect her confounding behavior: the very actress who portrays her in “The Dropout.” Fielder plays Seyfried a brutal clip from his time with Holmes, when he tries watching “The Dropout” with the subject of the series. When they get to a tense scene involving Holmes’ manipulative ex-boyfriend and former Theranos partner in crime Sunny Balwani — who is also now in prison — Holmes can no longer bear to watch this fictional version of herself. She turns away and cries. In other words, Seyfried is watching Holmes react to Seyfried’s portrayal of Holmes, who was probably also playing a character herself. But Seyfried is not the only one creating a crude approximation of the real Elizabeth. Evans has constructed a lifelike AI avatar of his wife, trapped inside of a large vertical screen that he wheels over to the dinner table to sit with him and his kids as though she’s actually there. The remainder of the film is a constellation of colliding personas. Though it’s a nonfiction documentary, it’s clear that everyone involved is, to some extent, also performing for the cameras. How could they not? Seyfried’s determination to understand Holmes’ story seems pure, but it’s not lost on the audience that she just scored a significant role in one of the most talked-about movies of the year. Meanwhile, Evans behaves in such an unfathomably egregious manner that he may even be intentionally playing the villain to drum up sympathy for his reviled wife. Evans knows that Fielder and Oppenheim are not convinced of Holmes’ innocence. This documentary will not sway anyone to believe that his wife is being wrongly held in federal custody. But Evans makes himself appear so appallingly unlikable that some viewers may leave the theater feeling bad for Holmes, seeing her as a victim and allowing her to double down on another persona she adopted while on trial: a harmless, docile woman who was manipulated by her ex-partner to obliviously tell a cascade of increasingly harmful lies. Once Holmes is in jail, Fielder is not allowed to bring recording devices when he visits her, so he tries to write a script of their conversations from memory, struggling to accurately re-create the nuances of a conversation where every last word carries immense meaning. With Seyfried reprising her role from “The Dropout,” we see the pair practice reading the script, editing the language as Fielder tries to recall Holmes’ exact phrasing and delivery. In character as Holmes, Seyfried says, “People think Amanda’s show is a documentary. passages: Movies don’t come much wilder than “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s brilliant, up-close-and-personal documentary about convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes that’s already the talker of the year.

So, he and Holmes invite oddball comedian Fielder of all people into their beach house rental in San Diego, Calif., to document the 34 days before she begins her 11-year prison sentence in Bryan, Texas.
Well, that bizarre choice has backfired for them, but it’s a seismically entertaining coup for us.
But Fielder even calls our antipathy toward Evans into question.
Fans of reality TV know that a season’s hero and the baddie can be determined, or at least amplified, in the editing room.
This is not a doc of straightforward revelations such as those of “The Jinx.” Nor is it a clear rundown of events, like the Holmes movie “ The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley ” was.
Most of Fielder’s time is spent from here on out with Evans, who we never like.

extraction.body: Running time: 174 minutes. Rated R (language and some graphic nudity). In theaters Movies don’t come much wilder than “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s brilliant, up-close-and-personal documentary about convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes that’s already the talker of the year. The Theranos founder with a husky voice and giant freaky eyes out of a Walter Keane painting has endlessly fascinated the world since her story was dramatized on the 2022 series “The Dropout” starring Amanda Seyfried. After that hit — a hit job in her estimation — Holmes became a party impression, a Halloween costume, an “SNL” joke and a dinner table topic. Whatever she is, most rational people believe that what she did — misleading the public and deep-pocketed investors that her “revolutionary” blood-testing device actually worked — was wrong. But not off-her-rocker Holmes and her equally delusional and sometimes downright villainous fiancé, Billy Evans, who we meet in this truly shocking and invasive film. This cuckoo couple’s credo is: innocent until well after proven guilty. Holmes, they say, is merely the victim of the court of public opinion. “Liz has been turned into this monster because nobody knows who she is,” Evans, lovable as a garden snake, says. Seizing a popular, touchy-feely word, he insists his betrothed has been “othered.” So, he and Holmes invite oddball comedian Fielder of all people into their beach house rental in San Diego, Calif., to document the 34 days before she begins her 11-year prison sentence in Bryan, Texas. Well, that bizarre choice has backfired for them, but it’s a seismically entertaining coup for us. Watching “You Can See Everything” is like being on Willy Wonka’s messed-up boat for three unbelievable hours. If the pair’s aim was to show that Holmes is perfectly normal, um, whoops! Over and over she stares frighteningly into the distance as if about to say, “Mr. DeMille, I’m ready for my closeup.” Occasionally a single tear cascades down her cheek as in the recent horror flick “ Other Mommy .” Sorry, “ Othered Mommy.” And while they do get the “human story” they hoped awkward, uncomfortable Fielder would deliver, he’s a rather deft and dogged interviewer with a truffle hound’s nose for a story. “Have you ever lied in your life?” he smartly asks her. Holmes, less of a human than “E.T.,” replies, “I don’t think so.” Fielder and Oppenheim’s sometimes funny, frequently chilling, visually stunning flick is unusual, to say the least. This is not a doc of straightforward revelations such as those of “The Jinx.” Nor is it a clear rundown of events, like the Holmes movie “ The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley ” was. This is an intrusive character study that, in a stimulating and riveting way, muddies the situation even more. We start to wonder: Has Holmes repeatedly fallen prey to bad men who take advantage of her charm, such as her ex-boyfriend and Theranos co-founder Sunny Balwani and, cough cough, others? Are her actions really their fault? Or does she gravitate toward those kinds of guys so they can act as an easy shield for her shrewd manipulations? Is she a nice girl led astray or a criminal mastermind? We’re even more mixed up as the camera’s focus goes to her adorable little children, a baby and a toddler. It’s hard not to feel sympathy for a young mother, or at least the kids who are about to be separated from her for more than a decade. If you know anything about prison, you know you can’t just take documentary cameras through the metal detector during visiting hours. So, once Holmes goes to the clink, Fielder and Oppenheim must get creative for the second half — resulting in some of the craziest stuff I’ve ever seen in a movie. Using transcripts from notes and memories, Fielder takes the old workhorse of documentary reenactments and gives it a novel twist. But what starts out as just a clever and fun idea warps into a dark, meta experiment that verges on a psychological thriller. If we were already questioning what’s real and what isn’t, it’s here when our brains explode and pool on the floor with the popcorn kernels and scattered Nerds. Most of Fielder’s time is spent from here on out with Evans, who we never like. But midway through, we begin to positively loathe him. The man, who’s mystifyingly working to exhume Theranos from the start-up cemetery, is soon to be the planet’s jackass du jour. A flagrant narcissist, he asks the camera crew to come film him working out at the gym. And, lending credence to the title, at one point we watch him taking a shower totally naked with full-frontal. But he’s also slimy with his partner. As Holmes is beating eggs, he snatches the bowl away because he doesn’t like her whisking technique. When Fielder presses her on her shady verbiage — that her machine “can” perform hundreds of blood tests, as opposed to “is capable of” doing so with the right chemistry advancements — Evans condescendingly jumps in to say, “You were communicating very clearly in your mind.” But Fielder even calls our antipathy toward Evans into question. Fans of reality TV know that a season’s hero and the baddie can be determined, or at least amplified, in the editing room. And at the end of “You Can See Everything,” Fielder and Oppenheim suggest that perhaps our trusty interviewer liked one of these two more than the other, and that preference seeped into his subconscious. Ding! Isn’t that exactly how this bewitching and fascinating woman became the youngest-ever self-made billionaire in the first place? The ultimate takeaway of this absolutely sensational, reality-bending, unmissable documentary? With Elizabeth Holmes, we will never see everything.

relevantPassages.text: Movies don’t come much wilder than “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s brilliant, up-close-and-personal documentary about convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes that’s already the talker of the year.

So, he and Holmes invite oddball comedian Fielder of all people into their beach house rental in San Diego, Calif., to document the 34 days before she begins her 11-year prison sentence in Bryan, Texas.
Well, that bizarre choice has backfired for them, but it’s a seismically entertaining coup for us.
But Fielder even calls our antipathy toward Evans into question.
Fans of reality TV know that a season’s hero and the baddie can be determined, or at least amplified, in the editing room.
This is not a doc of straightforward revelations such as those of “The Jinx.” Nor is it a clear rundown of events, like the Holmes movie “ The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley ” was.
Most of Fielder’s time is spent from here on out with Evans, who we never like.

sources.title: Israeli spyware targeted 'hundreds of millions' through zero-click ads, researchers find - Middle East Eye
passages: Millions of people's devices have been infected with Israeli commercial spyware called Candiru through zero-click digital advertisements, Canadian cyber watchdog group The Citizen Lab found in an investigation .

Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate ad company but in reality operates for Israeli spyware partners like Candiru, placed targeted ads that directed millions of devices in dozens of countries to contact Candiru's servers for tracking and reconnaissance, according to the report.
Candiru was also used to target Middle East Eye and other websites in November 2021.
The case marks the first zero-click mercenary spyware, confirmed publicly, delivered through targeted ads, the group said in a report published on Thursday.
The spyware also targeted devices linked to Al Jazeera Media Network.
ESET said that the targets had "links to the Middle East and a strong focus on Yemen and the surrounding conflict".

Discover-Tech controls a platform called Controlium that allows "mercenary partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices" as soon as the ad is shown, without having the target even click on it.
The attack, discovered by online security firm ESET, targeted MEE's website during two days in April 2020.

extraction.body: Millions of people's devices have been infected with Israeli commercial spyware called Candiru through zero-click digital advertisements, Canadian cyber watchdog group The Citizen Lab found in an investigation . The case marks the first zero-click mercenary spyware, confirmed publicly, delivered through targeted ads, the group said in a report published on Thursday. The spyware also targeted devices linked to Al Jazeera Media Network. Mercenary spyware is a highly advanced, custom-built form of malware created by private companies and sold to paying clients, including states. Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate ad company but in reality operates for Israeli spyware partners like Candiru, placed targeted ads that directed millions of devices in dozens of countries to contact Candiru's servers for tracking and reconnaissance, according to the report. The Citizen Lab found that in 2024 and 2025, at least 45 devices within Al Jazeera were targeted in a series of zero-click ad attacks purchased by Discover-Tech. Discover-Tech controls a platform called Controlium that allows "mercenary partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices" as soon as the ad is shown, without having the target even click on it. During a four-month period, Discover-Tech's ads were shown on almost 200,000 unique websites and Android/iOS apps in dozens of countries. Aside from Candiru, rebranded as Integrity Labs, Discover-Tech is also linked to other mercenary spyware actors, including Intelos and Bindecy. Candiru was blacklisted by the US government in 2021 for "engaging in activities contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States". Candiru's rebrand came after it was acquired by US private equity firm Integrity Partners in 2025, which is not sanctioned by the US. Discover-Tech has appeared as a "certified and "approved" vendor operated by Google and the advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has placed ads in major networks including Google, the Russian search engine Yandex and the platform Beeswax. "The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat," Wolfie Cristl, a senior researcher at The Citizen Lab, told Reuters. "For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike." Jerome Dangu, cofounder of the New York advertising security firm Confiant, which also published a separate report on the case on Thursday, said that Discover-Tech was placing at least 10 million ads per day worldwide and that data-sharing arrangements - called cookie matching - allowed it to track people even beyond its advertisements' reach. "Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said. Dangu added that the ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. The Citizen Lab said it had also found Discover-Tech ad impressions in Nato and United Nations networks, as well as the European Parliament, European Commission and more than a dozen national governments. Ads also appeared in media organisations in eight countries including Australia, Mexico and Europe. Israeli spyware firm NSO Group was also added to the US trade blacklist, along with Candiru, in November 2021, after the US concluded that foreign governments had bought its spyware and used it to target government officials, journalists, and others. Candiru was also used to target Middle East Eye and other websites in November 2021. The attack, discovered by online security firm ESET, targeted MEE's website during two days in April 2020. The campaign targeted 20 other websites in two waves: April to July 2020 and January to August 2021. ESET said that the targets had "links to the Middle East and a strong focus on Yemen and the surrounding conflict". Following findings by the two research groups, Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, and other platforms have since disconnected Discover-Tech's access to the digital advertising market. sources.title: How Israeli firm’s ‘zero-click’ malware attack poses global security risk - Al Jazeera
passages: An Israeli spyware firm has been found to be behind the first-known instance of “zero-click” targeted advertising in which fraudsters or spies can steal private data and send it to external servers, with Al Jazeera journalists among the victims.
Analysts say the findings are “incredibly concerning”, as they confirm the existence of a new global security threat.
“We knew we were headed in this direction and now it is out in the public,” Remesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies at the University of California in Los Angeles, US, told Al Jazeera.
Its advertisement network identified Al Jazeera staff, then quietly redirected them to an infected server belonging to Candiru.

The spyware firm was blacklisted by the US government in 2021, when Citizen Lab found it was responsible for the illegal hacking and surveillance of at least 100 activists , journalists and political activists across 10 countries.
Al Jazeera’s in-house technology team first discovered unusual patterns on devices used by some journalists in 2024.
Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera in 2025 provided a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed.
Just visiting a page or refreshing an app can be enough to fall victim to a malware attack in which your personal data is stolen from a laptop or phone, researchers have found.
Cybersecurity analyst and author Eddy Willems said the advertisements used automatically infect devices the moment they pop up on the screen, but there is an important technical nuance.
“Anyone with a phone or browser that shows ads can be reached, without the attacker needing their phone number or email.”
A new ‘zero-click’ hack uses ads to target victims without any action needed on their part.
The analyst said the risk remains low for most people as these attacks are expensive and aimed at specific targets.

Malicious advertisements were bought by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company presenting itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but which actually operates as a facilitator for mercenary spyware partners.

In a separate report, New York-based advertising security firm Confiant said its own investigations had found that some of Discover-Tech’s advertisements also appeared in critical networks used by the Pentagon, the United Nations International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court.

extraction.body: A new ‘zero-click’ hack uses ads to target victims without any action needed on their part. Just visiting a page or refreshing an app can be enough to fall victim to a malware attack in which your personal data is stolen from a laptop or phone, researchers have found. You are not even required to “click” on anything. An Israeli spyware firm has been found to be behind the first-known instance of “zero-click” targeted advertising in which fraudsters or spies can steal private data and send it to external servers, with Al Jazeera journalists among the victims. In June 2025, 45 devices used by Al Jazeera staff – including several who reported on sensitive subjects – were targeted with spyware which installed itself without the need to open or download any files. An investigation by the Canada-based academic research unit Citizen Lab, prompted by Al Jazeera’s initial internal probe into the issue, discovered that the Israeli company Candiru was behind the attacks. Analysts say the findings are “incredibly concerning”, as they confirm the existence of a new global security threat. “We knew we were headed in this direction and now it is out in the public,” Remesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies at the University of California in Los Angeles, US, told Al Jazeera. “This is the next level, because people are being microtargeted,” he said. “This is the point we’ve come to when it comes to surveillance.” Al Jazeera’s in-house technology team first discovered unusual patterns on devices used by some journalists in 2024. Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera in 2025 provided a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed. Malicious advertisements were bought by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company presenting itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but which actually operates as a facilitator for mercenary spyware partners. Its advertisement network identified Al Jazeera staff, then quietly redirected them to an infected server belonging to Candiru. The spyware firm was blacklisted by the US government in 2021, when Citizen Lab found it was responsible for the illegal hacking and surveillance of at least 100 activists , journalists and political activists across 10 countries. Al Jazeera Media Network has condemned the targeting of its staff members’ devices and called for those responsible to be held accountable. Cybersecurity analyst and author Eddy Willems said the advertisements used automatically infect devices the moment they pop up on the screen, but there is an important technical nuance. “Executing code inside the browser does not automatically give an attacker full control over the computer,” Willems told Al Jazeera. “To escape the browser’s isolated environment – the ‘sandbox’ – the attacker may need a second vulnerability,” Willems said, adding that an advanced spyware operation can combine several vulnerabilities. “The attacker attempts to exploit vulnerabilities to bypass security boundaries. This is precisely what makes this type of attack so dangerous,” the analyst said. Once the device is infected, the malicious software is designed to collect a wide range of sensitive data, including files, documents, and browser data such as cookies, bookmarks, and saved credentials. It can also capture keystrokes, take screenshots, record microphone and webcam input, and extract emails and messages from popular communication platforms. To avoid triggering security mechanisms, the spyware often uses encrypted communication channels and breaks up stolen data into smaller chunks sent over time. Analysts say Citizen Lab’s findings point to the escalation of an existing threat, which expands the scale and reach of traditional cyberattacks and makes them much harder to detect. While “zero-click” attacks are not completely new, the findings outline a new technique through which online advertisements are used as a route to infection. Stephen O’Shaughnessy, a lecturer in cybersecurity at the TU Dublin Blanchardstown campus in Ireland, explained that when a user opens a website or app, an automated auction sells the advertisement space in a fraction of a second. That auction shares data about the victim, including the device ID, IP address, rough location and the app or site they are on. “Discover-Tech posed as an ordinary advertiser, used that data to find their target and win the auction for that person’s screen,” O’Shaughnessy told Al Jazeera. “Anyone with a phone or browser that shows ads can be reached, without the attacker needing their phone number or email.” “Because no message or link is involved, there is almost nothing for the victim to notice,” he added. Discover-Tech appeared on lists of “certified” and “approved” vendors maintained by Google and advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has served advertisements via major networks such as Google, Yandex and Beeswax. In its report, Citizen Lab said this illustrates the structural flaws in the online advertising system, which essentially failed to detect or prevent the abuse. Discover-Tech advertisements have popped up on devices used by personnel in national-security-sensitive networks around the world, including those of various ministries of defence, armed forces, national cyber agencies, intergovernmental organisations and media outlets, Citizen Lab found. The research unit said these advertisements have also appeared on networks used by the United Nations, NATO, the European Parliament, the European Commission and the Council of the European Union’s General Secretariat. Government networks have also been targeted in at least 24 countries, including the United States, Italy, Denmark, Norway, Australia, Russia, Mexico and Israel itself. Networks of media organisations have also been targeted, mainly in Australia, Denmark and Sweden, according to Citizen Lab. In a separate report, New York-based advertising security firm Confiant said its own investigations had found that some of Discover-Tech’s advertisements also appeared in critical networks used by the Pentagon, the United Nations International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court. O’Shaughnessy said infection has not been confirmed there – only profiling of users. “But that alone is concerning, he said. “The ad system was built to send code from strangers to billions of screens with pinpoint targeting. Almost nobody was watching it from a security angle.” The analyst said the risk remains low for most people as these attacks are expensive and aimed at specific targets. “For individuals at high risk, like journalists and officials, the best first defence is to install an ad blocker, switch off their advertising ID through their phone’s privacy settings, keep everything updated, and turn on Lockdown Mode or Android’s Advanced Protection,” he said. Precautions also need to be taken within the industry and at government level. “To combat this, the ad industry needs to properly vet who’s buying ads,” O’Shaughnessy said, while “regulators need to stop personal data being sprayed out to thousands of unknown bidders in every auction.”

extraction.body: Millions of people's devices have been infected with Israeli commercial spyware called Candiru through zero-click digital advertisements, Canadian cyber watchdog group The Citizen Lab found in an investigation . The case marks the first zero-click mercenary spyware, confirmed publicly, delivered through targeted ads, the group said in a report published on Thursday. The spyware also targeted devices linked to Al Jazeera Media Network. Mercenary spyware is a highly advanced, custom-built form of malware created by private companies and sold to paying clients, including states. Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate ad company but in reality operates for Israeli spyware partners like Candiru, placed targeted ads that directed millions of devices in dozens of countries to contact Candiru's servers for tracking and reconnaissance, according to the report. The Citizen Lab found that in 2024 and 2025, at least 45 devices within Al Jazeera were targeted in a series of zero-click ad attacks purchased by Discover-Tech. Discover-Tech controls a platform called Controlium that allows "mercenary partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices" as soon as the ad is shown, without having the target even click on it. During a four-month period, Discover-Tech's ads were shown on almost 200,000 unique websites and Android/iOS apps in dozens of countries. Aside from Candiru, rebranded as Integrity Labs, Discover-Tech is also linked to other mercenary spyware actors, including Intelos and Bindecy. Candiru was blacklisted by the US government in 2021 for "engaging in activities contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States". Candiru's rebrand came after it was acquired by US private equity firm Integrity Partners in 2025, which is not sanctioned by the US. Discover-Tech has appeared as a "certified and "approved" vendor operated by Google and the advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has placed ads in major networks including Google, the Russian search engine Yandex and the platform Beeswax. "The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat," Wolfie Cristl, a senior researcher at The Citizen Lab, told Reuters. "For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike." Jerome Dangu, cofounder of the New York advertising security firm Confiant, which also published a separate report on the case on Thursday, said that Discover-Tech was placing at least 10 million ads per day worldwide and that data-sharing arrangements - called cookie matching - allowed it to track people even beyond its advertisements' reach. "Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said. Dangu added that the ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. The Citizen Lab said it had also found Discover-Tech ad impressions in Nato and United Nations networks, as well as the European Parliament, European Commission and more than a dozen national governments. Ads also appeared in media organisations in eight countries including Australia, Mexico and Europe. Israeli spyware firm NSO Group was also added to the US trade blacklist, along with Candiru, in November 2021, after the US concluded that foreign governments had bought its spyware and used it to target government officials, journalists, and others. Candiru was also used to target Middle East Eye and other websites in November 2021. The attack, discovered by online security firm ESET, targeted MEE's website during two days in April 2020. The campaign targeted 20 other websites in two waves: April to July 2020 and January to August 2021. ESET said that the targets had "links to the Middle East and a strong focus on Yemen and the surrounding conflict". Following findings by the two research groups, Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, and other platforms have since disconnected Discover-Tech's access to the digital advertising market. extraction.body: A new ‘zero-click’ hack uses ads to target victims without any action needed on their part. Just visiting a page or refreshing an app can be enough to fall victim to a malware attack in which your personal data is stolen from a laptop or phone, researchers have found. You are not even required to “click” on anything. An Israeli spyware firm has been found to be behind the first-known instance of “zero-click” targeted advertising in which fraudsters or spies can steal private data and send it to external servers, with Al Jazeera journalists among the victims. In June 2025, 45 devices used by Al Jazeera staff – including several who reported on sensitive subjects – were targeted with spyware which installed itself without the need to open or download any files. An investigation by the Canada-based academic research unit Citizen Lab, prompted by Al Jazeera’s initial internal probe into the issue, discovered that the Israeli company Candiru was behind the attacks. Analysts say the findings are “incredibly concerning”, as they confirm the existence of a new global security threat. “We knew we were headed in this direction and now it is out in the public,” Remesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies at the University of California in Los Angeles, US, told Al Jazeera. “This is the next level, because people are being microtargeted,” he said. “This is the point we’ve come to when it comes to surveillance.” Al Jazeera’s in-house technology team first discovered unusual patterns on devices used by some journalists in 2024. Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera in 2025 provided a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed. Malicious advertisements were bought by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company presenting itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but which actually operates as a facilitator for mercenary spyware partners. Its advertisement network identified Al Jazeera staff, then quietly redirected them to an infected server belonging to Candiru. The spyware firm was blacklisted by the US government in 2021, when Citizen Lab found it was responsible for the illegal hacking and surveillance of at least 100 activists , journalists and political activists across 10 countries. Al Jazeera Media Network has condemned the targeting of its staff members’ devices and called for those responsible to be held accountable. Cybersecurity analyst and author Eddy Willems said the advertisements used automatically infect devices the moment they pop up on the screen, but there is an important technical nuance. “Executing code inside the browser does not automatically give an attacker full control over the computer,” Willems told Al Jazeera. “To escape the browser’s isolated environment – the ‘sandbox’ – the attacker may need a second vulnerability,” Willems said, adding that an advanced spyware operation can combine several vulnerabilities. “The attacker attempts to exploit vulnerabilities to bypass security boundaries. This is precisely what makes this type of attack so dangerous,” the analyst said. Once the device is infected, the malicious software is designed to collect a wide range of sensitive data, including files, documents, and browser data such as cookies, bookmarks, and saved credentials. It can also capture keystrokes, take screenshots, record microphone and webcam input, and extract emails and messages from popular communication platforms. To avoid triggering security mechanisms, the spyware often uses encrypted communication channels and breaks up stolen data into smaller chunks sent over time. Analysts say Citizen Lab’s findings point to the escalation of an existing threat, which expands the scale and reach of traditional cyberattacks and makes them much harder to detect. While “zero-click” attacks are not completely new, the findings outline a new technique through which online advertisements are used as a route to infection. Stephen O’Shaughnessy, a lecturer in cybersecurity at the TU Dublin Blanchardstown campus in Ireland, explained that when a user opens a website or app, an automated auction sells the advertisement space in a fraction of a second. That auction shares data about the victim, including the device ID, IP address, rough location and the app or site they are on. “Discover-Tech posed as an ordinary advertiser, used that data to find their target and win the auction for that person’s screen,” O’Shaughnessy told Al Jazeera. “Anyone with a phone or browser that shows ads can be reached, without the attacker needing their phone number or email.” “Because no message or link is involved, there is almost nothing for the victim to notice,” he added. extraction.body: A security guard has been charged with murder after police said he shot and killed a man who was smashing a jewelry kiosk at a Fort Worth shopping center. Tyron Henton, 31, was taken into custody by Fort Worth police on Friday in connection with the Oct. 14 shooting at the La Gran Plaza shopping mall, records show. According to previous reports, Henton was working inside the shopping center when he saw a man smashing a kiosk with a blunt object. Henton opened fire, striking the man, who then ran across the parking lot and collapsed near Seminary Drive, officials said. Responding officers said the man died soon after they arrived on scene, just before 9 p.m. No further information has been released regarding the incident. It’s unclear if Henton was employed by the shopping center or a private company.
