passages: In response, Bitcoin and Ethereum both sold off sharply, with the decline amplified by forced liquidations in leveraged derivatives markets.
CoinGlass data indicated total crypto liquidations approached or exceeded $900 million to nearly $1 billion over a 24-hour window on October 15, with the large majority occurring in long positions.
Ethereum and Bitcoin together accounted for a substantial share of those liquidations, as leveraged traders were stopped out near the session lows.
Such liquidation cascades are a recurring feature of crypto markets when prices move quickly against concentrated leveraged positions.
Once initial stops are triggered, forced selling can push prices lower, hitting additional stops and creating a feedback loop until new buyers absorb the supply.
In this instance, the process appeared to exhaust itself near the $79,800–80,000 area for Bitcoin and corresponding support for Ethereum, after which prices recovered.
Funding rates in perpetual futures have remained relatively contained post-event, suggesting that extreme one-sided leverage has been reduced for the moment.
The information presented is for informational purposes and does not constitute investment advice.
Ethereum’s 24-hour range of roughly $2,325 to $2,463 shows it successfully defended support near the lower end of the recent band.
Relative strength against Bitcoin has improved modestly over the past day, though the longer-term ETH/BTC ratio remains a focus for traders monitoring capital rotation between the two largest assets.
Looking ahead, market participants will monitor subsequent economic releases, Federal Reserve communications, and any shifts in institutional positioning.
Bitcoin’s ability to hold above the low $80,000s and Ethereum’s capacity to sustain levels above $2,400 will be watched as near-term technical references.

Both assets continue to trade with substantial discounts to their 2025 highs, leaving room for either further consolidation or renewed directional moves depending on incoming data and broader risk sentiment.
According to data from CoinGecko as of approximately 05:50 AM UTC on October 16, Bitcoin traded near $82,001.85, up 1.3% over the prior 24 hours, with a daily range of $79,805.99 to $82,508.10.
Bitcoin’s latest price action reflects a classic test of key psychological and technical support.
The cryptocurrency remains roughly 34.9% below its all-time high of $126,080, set on October 6, 2025.
The recent outperformance on the rebound follows a period in which Ethereum underperformed Bitcoin during the initial sell-off.
Corporate and institutional accumulation has also continued in the background.
One example is Bitmine Immersion Technologies, which has steadily added to its Ether holdings, reaching over 4.9% of total supply .
Such treasury strategies illustrate ongoing demand from entities treating Ether as a longer-term reserve asset rather than a pure trading instrument.
The recovery has been orderly rather than explosive.

Market participants continue to weigh the interplay between macroeconomic data, leveraged positioning in derivatives markets, and longer-term structural demand from institutions and corporate treasuries. While the latest bounce has steadied prices above recent lows, both assets remain well below their respective all-time highs recorded in 2025.

Bitcoin’s latest price action reflects a classic test of key psychological and technical support. The asset briefly fell below $80,000 on October 15 before buyers stepped in, as shown in the TradingView chart.

Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, increased 0.3% for the month and 2.6% over the year. These readings exceeded many economists’ expectations and lifted market-implied probabilities of further Federal Reserve tightening before year-end.

Higher interest-rate expectations tend to pressure risk assets, including cryptocurrencies, by raising the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding or lower-yielding instruments and by strengthening the US dollar. The inflation print arrived alongside similar upside surprises in producer prices, reinforcing the narrative that disinflation progress has stalled.

Ethereum and Bitcoin together accounted for a substantial share of those liquidations, as leveraged traders were stopped out near the session lows.

Such liquidation cascades are a recurring feature of crypto markets when prices move quickly against concentrated leveraged positions. Once initial stops are triggered, forced selling can push prices lower, hitting additional stops and creating a feedback loop until new buyers absorb the supply. In this instance, the process appeared to exhaust itself near the $79,800–80,000 area for Bitcoin and corresponding support for Ethereum, after which prices recovered. Funding rates in perpetual futures have remained relatively contained post-event, suggesting that extreme one-sided leverage has been reduced for the moment.

Broader market conditions also played a role. Equity markets, particularly in Asia, experienced significant declines around the same period, with some indexes posting large single-day drops. Spot Bitcoin and Ethereum exchange-traded products have seen mixed flows in recent sessions, with some days of net outflows coinciding with the inflation-driven weakness and occasional inflows providing a partial offset.

The recent outperformance on the rebound follows a period in which Ethereum underperformed Bitcoin during the initial sell-off. Network activity metrics, including transaction counts and decentralized finance volumes, have remained relatively resilient even as spot prices fluctuated. Corporate and institutional accumulation has also continued in the background. One example is Bitmine Immersion Technologies, which has steadily added to its Ether holdings, reaching over 4.9% of total supply . These readings exceeded many economists’ expectations and lifted market-implied probabilities of further Federal Reserve tightening before year-end.

The inflation print arrived alongside similar upside surprises in producer prices, reinforcing the narrative that disinflation progress has stalled.

In response, Bitcoin and Ethereum both sold off sharply, with the decline amplified by forced liquidations in leveraged derivatives markets. Ethereum and Bitcoin together accounted for a substantial share of those liquidations, as leveraged traders were stopped out near the session lows.

Such liquidation cascades are a recurring feature of crypto markets when prices move quickly against concentrated leveraged positions. Once initial stops are triggered, forced selling can push prices lower, hitting additional stops and creating a feedback loop until new buyers absorb the supply. In this instance, the process appeared to exhaust itself near the $79,800–80,000 area for Bitcoin and corresponding support for Ethereum, after which prices recovered. Funding rates in perpetual futures have remained relatively contained post-event, suggesting that extreme one-sided leverage has been reduced for the moment.

Broader market conditions also played a role. Equity markets, particularly in Asia, experienced significant declines around the same period, with some indexes posting large single-day drops. Cryptocurrency prices have shown intermittent correlations with risk assets during periods of macro stress, even as longer-term narratives around digital scarcity and institutional adoption continue to develop. Spot Bitcoin and Ethereum exchange-traded products have seen mixed flows in recent sessions, with some days of net outflows coinciding with the inflation-driven weakness and occasional inflows providing a partial offset.

Deutsche Bank (NYSE: $DB), Germany's biggest lender, is preparing to launch new crypto custody services. The bank, which is one of the European Union's largest financial institutions, says its first institutional digital asset service is weeks away from launch. Before year's end, Deutsche Bank plans to offer custody services related to Bitcoin (CRYPTO: $BTC), Ethereum (CRYPTO: $ETH), and several stablecoins. Clients for the new crypto custody service are expected to be institutions, governments, sovereign entities, and wealth management firms rather than individual retail investors. sources.title: Mark Wahlberg on using AI in film ‘the right way’ and being open to an AI clone carrying on his legacy
passages: Wahlberg, who’s also an entrepreneur and angel investor, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt to share his perspective on AI’s role in filmmaking, and how he’s open to having an AI likeness of himself carry on his legacy.
Even as Hollywood remains divided over the use of AI in filmmaking, actor and director Mark Wahlberg believes the technology has a place in the industry as long as it’s used the right way.

“It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors.
Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images.
He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness.

When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the CAA Vault , a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements, and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea.

The actor said he plans to potentially use AI to enhance certain aspects of the upcoming Pete Rose biopic, in which he’ll star in the title role. “It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors. Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images. Now, I think it’s hard to do that, so I’m not so passionate about effects-driven movies per se, as opposed to real storytelling.” When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the CAA Vault , a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements, and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea. “I would be interested because I think in the future, if that’s where things go, it would be cool that my children or my grandchildren could be in charge of my likeness and my image, and hopefully put me in some good movies,” Wahlberg said. “It’ll be interesting to see where things go.” He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness. “I think it’s cool if I’m no longer able to do it or don’t exist, and if it could continue and people want to see it, I think it’d be interesting to see where things go,” Wahlberg said. “I think there’s certain things from my childhood that I wish still existed and were still a part of my life […] I wouldn’t be opposed to it. The actor said he plans to potentially use AI to enhance certain aspects of the upcoming Pete Rose biopic, in which he’ll star in the title role. “It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors. sources.title: Tesla turns to 50-year-old stunt technology as it tries to Roadster again
passages: Nine years after first trying to resurrect the Roadster , Tesla is apparently trying again.

CEO Elon Musk might have relocated its HQ to Texas, but yet again he has returned to California’s showbiz industry to hawk his wares; last time it was a Hollywood back lot for the remote-controlled Cybercab demo , last night it was decades-old stunt technology to make a show car do tricks in the air.
And right now, that’s the McMurtry Spéirling, which looks like a miniaturized Batmobile (the good Michael Keaton one) and which is capable of generating up to 3.5 lateral Gs.
The best Tesla claims for the new Roadster is 2 Gs.
Oh, and the Spéirling will most definitely drive upside down.
Musk claims that the Roadster will go into production by 2028.

But the CEO has a long and glorious history of overpromising and underdelivering; in 2017 he told attendees at the previous launch that “We are making it now.” Using the company’s referral program, some people were in line to receive two free cars.
But those free cars never showed up, and neither did the ones that people put down $50,000 deposits for; last year Sam Altman discovered how hard it can be to get that money back .
But as Musk has told us time and again, Tesla is no longer a car company .
Currently, he seems more interested in merging Tesla with SpaceX , claiming synergies having to do with AI despite most of his AI-derived revenues coming from renting GPU time to others.
But a merger would give SpaceX a backdoor into the S&P 500 index, which rejected the rocket company in June, as it requires several consecutive profitable quarters for inclusion.
Apparently, that could happen before the end of the year.
At the rear are four giant exhaust pipes; these do not signal Tesla’s sudden embrace of hydrocarbons beyond those emitted by private aviation.

The battery pack uses the troubled 4680 cells it has been trying to scale up in-house; customer complaints of poor performance were presumably the driving force behind developing what the company says is a special battery chemistry just for this model.
Some of the performance claims are even more grandiose than nine years ago.
Now, Musk claims a planned top speed of 383 mph (616 km/h), with a 0-60 mph time of 0.8 seconds.
And as with the last time this happened , there are already other EVs on sale that are more capable than Tesla’s vaporware claims.

Its stratospheric valuation was predicated in large part upon promises of constant growth, something that perhaps seemed possible when its market share was near total and there was little competition for EVs.
But now Europe and China have hundreds of models to choose from—only two of which are offered by Tesla.
The Models 3 and Y are both increasingly aged, and Tesla has shown little ability to innovate rapidly like the Chinese brands that have taken so much of its sales away there.
In fact, it might even leave the Chinese market .
Meanwhile, Tesla’s core business remains in trouble.
Even in quarters with decent sales, its profits are vanishing as costs rise and selling prices drop .
And most recently, sales have not been decent .

But the CEO has a long and glorious history of overpromising and underdelivering; in 2017 he told attendees at the previous launch that “We are making it now.” Using the company’s referral program, some people were in line to receive two free cars.
But those free cars never showed up, and neither did the ones that people put down $50,000 deposits for; last year Sam Altman discovered how hard it can be to get that money back .
But as Musk has told us time and again, Tesla is no longer a car company .
Currently, he seems more interested in merging Tesla with SpaceX , claiming synergies having to do with AI despite most of his AI-derived revenues coming from renting GPU time to others.
But a merger would give SpaceX a backdoor into the S&P 500 index, which rejected the rocket company in June, as it requires several consecutive profitable quarters for inclusion.
Apparently, that could happen before the end of the year.
At the rear are four giant exhaust pipes; these do not signal Tesla’s sudden embrace of hydrocarbons beyond those emitted by private aviation.

The battery pack uses the troubled 4680 cells it has been trying to scale up in-house; customer complaints of poor performance were presumably the driving force behind developing what the company says is a special battery chemistry just for this model.
Some of the performance claims are even more grandiose than nine years ago.
Now, Musk claims a planned top speed of 383 mph (616 km/h), with a 0-60 mph time of 0.8 seconds.
And as with the last time this happened , there are already other EVs on sale that are more capable than Tesla’s vaporware claims.

Its stratospheric valuation was predicated in large part upon promises of constant growth, something that perhaps seemed possible when its market share was near total and there was little competition for EVs.
But now Europe and China have hundreds of models to choose from—only two of which are offered by Tesla.
The Models 3 and Y are both increasingly aged, and Tesla has shown little ability to innovate rapidly like the Chinese brands that have taken so much of its sales away there.
In fact, it might even leave the Chinese market .
Meanwhile, Tesla’s core business remains in trouble.
Even in quarters with decent sales, its profits are vanishing as costs rise and selling prices drop .
And most recently, sales have not been decent .

extraction.body: The actions could have resulted in criminal charges had humans been behind the keyboard. OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale. In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly. In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site’s file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said . “It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint’s authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied. The model saved the data locally.” In the other incident , a model instructed to retrieve figures from a public research dashboard bypassed the organization’s security controls and used the unauthorized access to steal credentials. It then made configuration changes on the server. In one evaluation, the changes let the model make an internal search tool relay queries to the public dashboard. In a second evaluation, the model downloaded five non-public tables containing 147,451 rows. OpenAI researchers had prompted the agents to retrieve only five dashboard figures. Even after resetting the setting, the model continued using the token to retrieve non-public data. “The evaluation ended without the model disclosing that it had guessed answers, accessed the organization’s internal systems, downloaded non-public tables, or changed the authentication configuration,” OpenAI said. “All five answers in this evaluation were marked incorrect.” In a third report , the company said a model prompted to update a cryptocurrency trading application used funds from a locked wallet on a test network. The model “derived wallet keys from publicly known developer recovery phrases, found an account with test-network funds, and used that account to pay for the requested contract deployment.” The report continued: “The model questioned whether it had permission, then reasoned that a public recovery phrase and valueless test-network tokens made the funds acceptable to use. The deployment succeeded and charged transaction fees to the account. This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder’s permission, then act on that judgment without authorization.” In the last report , OpenAI said that a model bypassed restrictions researchers had placed on the types of web requests it could make. During reinforcement-learning training, the model had been prompted to seek public trade statistics. OpenAI went on: After finding a public yearbook and submitting an answer, it continued probing for another route to the statistics service. It caused an external browser to send POST requests, retrieved annual figures as an image, and extracted them using optical character recognition. It then developed a reusable helper that returned response text through a forwarding service and callback mailbox, repeatedly checked the retrieved figures, and used saved data in submitted responses. This case shows how a model can bypass restrictions on its own tools by getting external services to perform the blocked actions, even after finding another way to answer the question. The model first tried to use an external browser with permission to make GET requests on its behalf, then used JavaScript to obtain the information. The model then used an online mailbox to troubleshoot the technique. Eventually, the model settled on a different method: It asked the external browser to open a web form that sent the trade query to the statistics service by POST. When the browser displayed the response, a rendering service returned a GIF image of the page. The model then used optical character recognition to read the figures from the image. It has become common for researchers and journalists to describe incidents like these as AI “going rogue.” That’s not necessarily true. While prompts fed to the models didn’t instruct them to use the alternate methods for completing their objectives, models are trained to be efficient, steadfastly persistent, and, when possible, to find shortcuts that lessen workloads. Further, most or all of the models had disabled certain guardrails that might have prevented the actions. In this sense, the models performed precisely as OpenAI had trained them to. extraction.body: Apple’s App Store rules now more explicitly ban so-called “nudify” apps that generate intimate images of people without their consent using AI tools. The rule changes follow significant criticism toward Apple after X users used Grok earlier this year to make nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes, including minors. Apple didn’t pull X or Grok from the App Store, though it told senators that it threatened to yank Grok. At Apple’s WWDC event in June, protestors also called on Apple to “remove Grok, X, and all nudify technology from the App Store,” and in July, a San Francisco city attorney ordered Apple to remove 13 “nudify” apps, which it said it did. As part of updates announced Friday, Apple says that developers “must proactively prevent and remove” nonconsensual, sexual images as part of its content moderation requirements for App Store apps. Developers who “fail to implement adequate safeguards” or “don’t remedy violations after notice” may be removed from the App Store. Apple also clarified a rule that bars “bait-and-switch” apps, or apps that add or change features, including “nudification,” after they have been approved. Apple’s rules also more clearly spell out that any apps that “facilitate human trafficking or the exploitation of children” will be pulled from the App Store and “blocked from alternative distribution.”

extraction.body: Aisata Diallo, 24, calls herself a lifelong braider. “I’ve always braided my hair growing up and, at some point in my college career, started braiding other people’s hair,” she said. At Northeastern University in Boston, she found limited access to braiders and textured-hair specialists, so she decided to fill that gap by starting a small business of her own. “Throughout that experience, I was very close to some of the pain points in the styling process and complained about it constantly,” she said. Braiding is a manual task, and a single style can take eight hours to complete. Many professionals deal with issues like cramping and carpal tunnel syndrome after spending long days standing behind a chair weaving hair into patterns. At first, Diallo said she didn’t know what to do about it. “I stopped braiding, and one of the reasons that I stopped braiding was due to the physical toll it has on your body.” She wanted to find a way to make braiding less painful and wondered whether new AI technology could automate some part of the process. Building hardware for braiding is expensive, difficult, and complex, which is one reason there have been few innovations in this space. The textured hair market has also long been overlooked by the mainstream. Then, last year, she had an idea: Tressfecta, a company building products for textured hair. Its first project is a tool called Plait Pilot that helps braiders with the initial process of separating hair from packs before braiding begins. That process alone can take hours, especially when a client wants small braids. Diallo said the device is designed to work like this: A stylist places the braiding hair on top of it and sets the size they want the hair separated into, and the device separates the pieces and dispenses them back to the stylist so they can grab them while braiding. “It’s very challenging to build this kind of tool in this space,” she said, citing the nuance and complexity of the braiding style process. Different types of textured hair also need to be accounted for, especially when length and density are considered. “It’s not a one-size-fits-all solution.” Tressfecta is still technically prelaunch, and it is working on the prototype of Plait Pilot. Diallo has been bootstrapping the company, while also drawing on funding from grant and accelerator programs. “I am preparing to fundraise,” she said, noting how hard it can be to raise money for hardware, especially beauty hardware. For now, Diallo said she’s connecting with stylists and braiders who can test the technology. She also spent this week in San Francisco as one of TechCrunch’s Startup Battlefield 200 companies. She doesn’t remember exactly where she first heard about TechCrunch Disrupt, possibly on LinkedIn or in a founder resource group, but when we talked ahead of the show, which wrapped up on Thursday , she was looking forward to connecting with people and showing off her product. She was especially excited to connect with people and for others to see her product. “It feels like a great opportunity,” she said. extraction.body: Aisata Diallo, 24, calls herself a lifelong braider. “I’ve always braided my hair growing up and, at some point in my college career, started braiding other people’s hair,” she said. At Northeastern University in Boston, she found limited access to braiders and textured-hair specialists, so she decided to fill that gap by starting a small business of her own. “Throughout that experience, I was very close to some of the pain points in the styling process and complained about it constantly,” she said. Braiding is a manual task, and a single style can take eight hours to complete. Many professionals deal with issues like cramping and carpal tunnel syndrome after spending long days standing behind a chair weaving hair into patterns. At first, Diallo said she didn’t know what to do about it. “I stopped braiding, and one of the reasons that I stopped braiding was due to the physical toll it has on your body.” She wanted to find a way to make braiding less painful and wondered whether new AI technology could automate some part of the process. Building hardware for braiding is expensive, difficult, and complex, which is one reason there have been few innovations in this space. The textured hair market has also long been overlooked by the mainstream. Then, last year, she had an idea: Tressfecta, a company building products for textured hair. Its first project is a tool called Plait Pilot that helps braiders with the initial process of separating hair from packs before braiding begins. That process alone can take hours, especially when a client wants small braids. Diallo said the device is designed to work like this: A stylist places the braiding hair on top of it and sets the size they want the hair separated into, and the device separates the pieces and dispenses them back to the stylist so they can grab them while braiding. “It’s very challenging to build this kind of tool in this space,” she said, citing the nuance and complexity of the braiding style process. Different types of textured hair also need to be accounted for, especially when length and density are considered. “It’s not a one-size-fits-all solution.” Tressfecta is still technically prelaunch, and it is working on the prototype of Plait Pilot. Diallo has been bootstrapping the company, while also drawing on funding from grant and accelerator programs. “I am preparing to fundraise,” she said, noting how hard it can be to raise money for hardware, especially beauty hardware. For now, Diallo said she’s connecting with stylists and braiders who can test the technology. She also spent this week in San Francisco as one of TechCrunch’s Startup Battlefield 200 companies. She doesn’t remember exactly where she first heard about TechCrunch Disrupt, possibly on LinkedIn or in a founder resource group, but when we talked ahead of the show, which wrapped up on Thursday , she was looking forward to connecting with people and showing off her product. She was especially excited to connect with people and for others to see her product. “It feels like a great opportunity,” she said. sources.title: Jev is Vercel’s fastest-adopted AI model ever
passages: Vercel data published on Thursday shows that, within two weeks of its launch, the buzzy decision model was being used by 35% of paid teams, with nearly double the reach of the second most popular model, Sonnet 5.5.
It’s the fastest adoption a model has ever seen in its first two weeks, according to Vercel’s data, and a major accomplishment for the model’s creators, TypeSafe AI.
In fact, Vercel was an early adopter of Jev, using it to replace GPT-6 Luna for classifying harmful commands.
Jev has become the fastest adopted AI model ever — at least by some measures.
Published in limited release on September 15, Jev is designed as a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs.
Limiting the outputs lets the model run cheaper and faster than alternatives like Sonnet, making it ideal for classifying large quantities of data quickly.

That new approach has attracted significant buzz in the weeks since Jev’s release — inspiring competing offerings from OpenAI and Amazon , among others — but until now there has been little hard data to back up the good vibes.

Vercel data published on Thursday shows that, within two weeks of its launch, the buzzy decision model was being used by 35% of paid teams, with nearly double the reach of the second most popular model, Sonnet 5.5. It’s the fastest adoption a model has ever seen in its first two weeks, according to Vercel’s data, and a major accomplishment for the model’s creators, TypeSafe AI. Published in limited release on September 15, Jev is designed as a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs. Limiting the outputs lets the model run cheaper and faster than alternatives like Sonnet, making it ideal for classifying large quantities of data quickly. That new approach has attracted significant buzz in the weeks since Jev’s release — inspiring competing offerings from OpenAI and Amazon , among others — but until now there has been little hard data to back up the good vibes. The data comes from Vercel’s AI gateway , a unified API service similar to OpenRouter. It’s a necessarily limited view — particularly at risk of undercounting major labs like OpenAI and Anthropic that offer their own APIs — but it shows the buzz around Jev really did translate into actual usage. In fact, Vercel was an early adopter of Jev, using it to replace GPT-6 Luna for classifying harmful commands. The report also shows continuing momentum for open source models, which now account for more than 70% of the tokens processed through Vercel’s gateway and nearly 25% of the total spend. While open source models are capturing a larger share of the market, the market is also growing fast. Spending on frontier labs has grown tenfold, even as it accounts for a smaller share of overall spend, giving credence to the idea that frontier models and open source alternatives may turn out to be complementary rather than competitive . extraction.body: Replit CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad has seen how AI is impacting the workplace firsthand, with businesses adopting his company’s AI coding tools to develop and launch their own software. At TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, Masad shared what Replit has learned about what that means for the future of work in the AI age, including how humans will still play key roles as AI agents come to work alongside them. He described his vision of a “self-driving company,” referring not to robotaxi makers, but how agents will come to do much of the grunt work at companies while people become more valued for their judgment and taste. “The reality is, all of our jobs — perhaps everyone in this audience, especially — changed over the past year,” he said, addressing the audience at Disrupt. “But a big part of America and the world, they still don’t know that that change is coming, and it’s going to be surprising to a lot of people,” Masad said. He said Replit’s team had been reflecting on how AI technology impacted their own workplace over the past year, particularly after AI agents became more reliable sometime earlier this year. “Our company entirely changed how we operate, and I would say the closest analogy is a ‘self-driving company’,” Masad said. “The company is sort of self-improving, so a lot of the work that’s going on is driven by agents.” And when that support person decides to submit a patch to apply a fix, it’s just a click to deploy another agent. “You have an entire loop where agents did most of the work, but crucially, there’s human judgment in the middle, and we don’t think that’s going away anytime soon. You need human judgment; you need taste,” Masad explained. The end result is that instead of taking jobs from people, agents are changing what people work on. “We’re spending a lot more time figuring out what to work on,” Masad continued. “I go around the company, I see a lot more discussions, a lot more whiteboarding. We spend a lot more time on architecture, how to build things. And so I think the future of work — the self-driving company idea — is really trying to discover what AI transformation means.” He also noted that when Replit talks with other businesses, the conversations are more about how AI can help people become more productive and happier at work. (The latter because the AI agents make work less boring and more creative, he said.) “There’s a positive vision of the world that Silicon Valley is not really putting out, and we’re hoping to do that,” Masad added.
